title: NREMT EMT Cognitive Exam
blurb: The real NREMT EMT cognitive exam is computer-adaptive: it delivers between 70 and 120 items in a 2-hour window and stops as soon as it is 95% confident you are above or below the passing standard. Items are drawn from five content areas - Airway, Respiration and Ventilation; Cardiology and Resuscitation; Trauma; Medical, Obstetrics and Gynecology; and EMS Operations - with about 85% of patients adults and about 15% pediatric. This practice exam is not adaptive, but every attempt draws 100 fresh items from the pool using the real content weights, so the mix you see matches the mix the real test pulls from.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes the difference between ventilation and respiration?
choices: Ventilation is gas exchange at the cell; respiration is air movement
Ventilation is the mechanical movement of air in and out of the lungs; respiration is the exchange of gases
Ventilation and respiration are interchangeable terms for breathing
Ventilation occurs only in the alveoli; respiration occurs only in the trachea
questions.why: Ventilation is the physical movement of air into and out of the lungs, while respiration is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide at the alveolar-capillary membrane and at the cellular level. The reversed definition is a classic student error, and the two terms are not interchangeable because a patient can ventilate adequately yet fail to respire, as in carbon monoxide poisoning. The trachea is a conducting airway where no gas exchange occurs at all.

questions.q: A patient has a tidal volume of 500 mL and a respiratory rate of 12 breaths per minute. What is the minute volume?
choices: 600 mL
questions.why: Minute volume equals tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate, so 500 mL times 12 equals 6,000 mL per minute. The 600 mL and 1,200 mL answers come from dividing or from multiplying only part of the values. Minute volume matters more than rate alone, because a fast rate with a tiny tidal volume moves mostly dead-space air.

questions.q: Air that fills the trachea and bronchi but never reaches the alveoli for gas exchange is known as:
choices: Residual volume
Tidal volume
Dead space air
Reserve volume
questions.why: Dead space is the volume of each breath that remains in the conducting airways and never participates in gas exchange. Residual volume is air left in the lungs after a maximal exhalation, and tidal volume is the full volume of a normal breath. This is why very shallow, rapid breathing is ineffective: nearly the whole breath is dead space.

questions.q: You are assessing a 44-year-old woman who is alert. Which finding MOST clearly indicates inadequate breathing?
choices: A rate of 8 per minute with shallow, irregular chest movement
Speaking in full sentences with clear lung sounds
Pink, warm, dry skin with a regular rate
A respiratory rate of 18 with equal chest rise
questions.why: A rate of 8 with shallow, irregular movement produces a minute volume far below what is needed, so this patient requires assisted ventilation with a bag-valve mask. A rate of 18 with equal chest rise, full-sentence speech, and pink warm dry skin are all signs of adequate breathing. Students often fixate on rate alone, but depth and quality of movement are equally important.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man is sitting upright, is anxious, and can speak only three or four words between breaths. His SpO2 is 90 percent. This presentation BEST describes:
choices: Respiratory arrest
Respiratory distress
Adequate breathing
Respiratory failure
questions.why: He is compensating with increased work of breathing and remains alert, which defines respiratory distress. Respiratory failure would show fatigue, altered mental status, and a falling rate or effort, and arrest means no breathing at all. He is not adequate, because he cannot speak full sentences and his saturation is below the 94 to 99 percent target.

questions.q: A child with a long history of asthma was working hard to breathe. He is now sleepy, quiet, and his chest barely moves. Which is the MOST appropriate next action?
choices: Apply a non-rebreather at 15 L/min and monitor
Have him use his metered-dose inhaler again
Begin assisted ventilation with a bag-valve mask and supplemental oxygen
Place him in a position of comfort and reassess in five minutes
questions.why: A quiet chest with decreasing effort and altered mental status signals respiratory failure moving toward arrest, so positive pressure ventilation is required now. A non-rebreather and a position of comfort do nothing for a patient who is no longer moving enough air, and a sleepy child cannot generate the inspiratory effort needed to deliver an inhaler dose. Failing to recognize the ominous quiet chest is one of the most dangerous misses in pediatric airway care.

questions.q: You find an unresponsive adult with no suspected trauma and snoring respirations. Which of the following is the FIRST action?
choices: Insert a nasopharyngeal airway
Suction the oropharynx for 15 seconds
Begin bag-valve-mask ventilation
Perform a head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver
questions.why: Snoring indicates the tongue is obstructing the airway, and the head-tilt, chin-lift is the simplest and fastest way to open the airway in a nontrauma patient. Adjuncts and ventilation follow after the airway is opened manually. Suctioning is for fluid, not for a tongue obstruction, and a blind 15-second suction wastes time and removes oxygen.

questions.q: An unresponsive patient was ejected from a vehicle and has gurgling respirations. Which airway maneuver is MOST appropriate?
choices: Jaw-thrust maneuver with manual in-line stabilization
Head-tilt, chin-lift
Hyperextension of the neck to open the airway
Log-roll to the prone position
questions.why: When spinal injury is suspected, the modified jaw thrust opens the airway without moving the cervical spine. Head-tilt, chin-lift and any hyperextension move the neck and are avoided here. Prone positioning does not clear an airway and prevents assessment and ventilation.

questions.q: You are suctioning an adult patient with copious vomit in the airway. Suctioning should be limited to no longer than:
choices: 30 seconds
60 seconds
10 to 15 seconds
2 to 3 seconds
questions.why: Suctioning in an adult is limited to 10 to 15 seconds per attempt because suction removes oxygen along with secretions and can cause hypoxia and bradycardia. Thirty or sixty seconds is far too long and is a common student error under pressure. Two to three seconds is unnecessarily brief and leaves the airway soiled.

questions.q: Which catheter and technique are MOST appropriate for suctioning thick vomit from the mouth of an adult?
choices: Soft French catheter inserted through the nose
Rigid tonsil-tip catheter, suctioning on the way out
Rigid tonsil-tip catheter with suction applied on insertion
Soft French catheter inserted to the level of the carina
questions.why: A rigid tonsil-tip handles thick secretions and particulate matter, and suction is applied only while withdrawing the catheter. Applying suction going in strips oxygen from the airway and can injure tissue. A soft French catheter clogs on vomit and is intended for the nose or a tracheostomy tube.

questions.q: You must suction a 6-month-old infant with thick nasal secretions. The MAXIMUM recommended suction time for this patient is about:
choices: 5 seconds
15 seconds
20 seconds
30 seconds
questions.why: Infants desaturate very quickly, so suction attempts are limited to about 5 seconds. The 10 to 15 second window applies to adults, and students often carry the adult number over to infants. Preoxygenate between attempts and watch for bradycardia, which signals hypoxia.

questions.q: When suctioning a child with a mechanical suction unit, the vacuum pressure should generally be limited to:
choices: -200 to -250 mmHg
-300 mmHg or higher
-20 to -40 mmHg
-80 to -120 mmHg
questions.why: Pediatric suctioning is typically limited to about -80 to -120 mmHg to avoid mucosal injury and atelectasis. Pressures of -200 mmHg or more are excessive for a child, and -20 to -40 mmHg is too weak to clear secretions. Most units let you set the vacuum level before you begin.

questions.q: An oropharyngeal airway is sized by measuring from:
choices: The tip of the nose to the earlobe
The corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw or earlobe
The chin to the suprasternal notch
The center of the lips to the thyroid cartilage
questions.why: An OPA is measured from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw or the earlobe. Nose-to-earlobe is the measurement for a nasopharyngeal airway, a common mix-up. An OPA that is too long can push the epiglottis over the glottis, and one that is too short can press the tongue back into the pharynx.

questions.q: You insert an oropharyngeal airway and the patient begins to gag and retch. Which of the following is the BEST action?
choices: Immediately remove the airway and be prepared to suction
Leave it in place because the airway is now secured
Push the airway in further past the gag point
Replace it with a larger oropharyngeal airway
questions.why: An intact gag reflex is a contraindication to an OPA, so it is removed immediately and suction is readied because gagging often leads to vomiting. Leaving it in or forcing it deeper risks aspiration and laryngospasm. A larger OPA makes the problem worse; a nasopharyngeal airway is the appropriate alternative if an adjunct is still needed.

questions.q: A semiconscious 30-year-old fell from a roof and has clear fluid draining from his nose and bruising behind his ears. Which airway adjunct is CONTRAINDICATED?
choices: Oropharyngeal airway
Bag-valve mask with an oral airway
Nasopharyngeal airway
Non-rebreather mask
questions.why: Raccoon eyes, Battle sign, and clear drainage suggest a basilar skull fracture, which is a contraindication to a nasopharyngeal airway because of the risk of intracranial placement. An OPA can be used if he tolerates it without gagging, and oxygen or bag-valve-mask support remains appropriate. The NPA is otherwise the adjunct of choice in a patient with a gag reflex.

questions.q: A nasopharyngeal airway is properly sized by measuring from the:
choices: Tip of the nose to the corner of the mouth
Bridge of the nose to the chin
Nostril to the angle of the clavicle
Nostril to the tip of the earlobe
questions.why: An NPA is measured from the nostril to the tip of the earlobe on the same side, and the diameter should be the largest that fits the nostril without blanching. Nose-to-mouth-corner is too short and will not bypass the tongue. The device is lubricated with water-soluble gel and inserted with the bevel toward the septum.

questions.q: A 70-year-old with COPD has an SpO2 of 88 percent and mild dyspnea while speaking in full sentences. Which oxygen delivery device is MOST appropriate to start?
choices: Nasal cannula at 2 to 4 L/min, titrated to effect
Bag-valve mask at 15 L/min
Non-rebreather at 15 L/min regardless of response
No oxygen, because oxygen suppresses hypoxic drive
questions.why: Current practice is to titrate oxygen to a target saturation of 94 to 99 percent, and a low-flow nasal cannula is the appropriate starting device for a patient with mild distress who is ventilating adequately. A bag-valve mask is for inadequate ventilation, and a flat 15 L/min non-rebreather overshoots the target in a patient who needs only a little. Withholding oxygen out of hypoxic drive fear is an outdated and dangerous misconception; never deny oxygen to a hypoxic patient.

questions.q: A nasal cannula delivers an approximate oxygen concentration of:
choices: 35 to 60 percent at 1 to 6 L/min
24 to 44 percent at 1 to 6 L/min
60 to 80 percent at 6 to 10 L/min
Up to 90 percent at 10 to 15 L/min
questions.why: A nasal cannula at 1 to 6 L/min delivers roughly 24 to 44 percent oxygen. The 35 to 60 percent range at 6 to 10 L/min belongs to the simple face mask, and up to 90 percent at 10 to 15 L/min describes the non-rebreather. Flows above 6 L/min by cannula dry and irritate the nasal mucosa without meaningfully raising the concentration.

questions.q: A non-rebreather mask should be run at which flow rate, and what must be verified before placing it on the patient?
choices: 6 to 10 L/min, with the mask warmed
15 to 25 L/min, with the reservoir deflated
4 to 6 L/min, with the side ports taped closed
10 to 15 L/min, with the reservoir bag inflated before application
questions.why: A non-rebreather runs at 10 to 15 L/min and the reservoir bag must be filled before the mask goes on the face, or the patient will draw against an empty bag. Flow of 6 to 10 L/min is the simple mask range and will let the reservoir collapse. Taping the side ports and deflating the reservoir both defeat the design of the device.

questions.q: Which device delivers a precise, specific oxygen concentration through interchangeable color-coded adapters?
choices: Simple face mask
Non-rebreather mask
Venturi mask
Partial rebreather mask
questions.why: A Venturi mask entrains a fixed ratio of room air to deliver a precise concentration, commonly 24, 28, 31, 35, 40, or 50 percent, and is used when tight control matters, such as in chronic CO2 retainers. Simple masks, non-rebreathers, and partial rebreathers all deliver variable concentrations that change with the patient's own inspiratory effort. The Venturi is generally an interfacility transport device for EMTs.

questions.q: A bag-valve mask attached to an oxygen reservoir and run at 15 L/min delivers approximately what oxygen concentration?
choices: Near 100 percent
About 21 percent
About 50 percent
About 75 percent
questions.why: A BVM with a reservoir at 15 L/min delivers nearly 100 percent oxygen. Without the reservoir attached the same device delivers only about 40 to 60 percent, and with no oxygen connected at all it delivers room air at 21 percent. Forgetting to attach or fill the reservoir is a frequent and consequential error.

questions.q: For most patients, oxygen should be titrated to maintain an oxygen saturation in which range?
choices: 88 to 92 percent
90 to 93 percent
100 percent at all times
94 to 99 percent
questions.why: Current guidelines target an SpO2 of 94 to 99 percent for most acutely ill patients, titrating oxygen up or down to stay in that window. Chasing a constant 100 percent exposes patients to the harms of hyperoxia without benefit. The 88 to 92 percent range is a hospital-based target for selected chronic CO2 retainers, not a field default.

questions.q: A full oxygen cylinder typically reads about 2,000 psi. At what pressure is the cylinder generally considered to be at the safe residual level and taken out of service for refill?
choices: 200 psi
500 psi
50 psi
questions.why: The safe residual pressure is about 200 psi, at which point the cylinder is changed out because flow can no longer be reliably delivered. Waiting until 50 psi risks running dry mid-transport and can allow contaminants into the cylinder. Swapping at 1,000 psi wastes a large amount of usable oxygen.

questions.q: Which of the following is the MOST important safety practice when handling oxygen cylinders?
choices: Store cylinders lying loose on the bench seat for quick access
Lubricate the regulator threads with petroleum jelly to ease attachment
Keep cylinders away from heat and never use grease or oil on the fittings
Open the valve slowly while pointing the port toward your partner
questions.why: Oxygen under pressure combined with a petroleum product can ignite, so grease, oil, and adhesive tape stay away from fittings, and cylinders are kept from heat sources. Loose cylinders become projectiles in a crash and must be secured. Never point the valve port toward anyone when cracking it open.

questions.q: You are ventilating an apneic adult with a pulse using a bag-valve mask. What is the correct rate and volume?
choices: One breath every 6 seconds, just enough for visible chest rise
One breath every 3 seconds, until the chest rises sharply
Two breaths every 5 seconds, delivered forcefully
One breath every 10 seconds, squeezing the bag fully
questions.why: Adult rescue breathing for a patient with a pulse is one breath every 6 seconds, or 10 per minute, each delivered over about one second to visible chest rise. One every 3 seconds is the pediatric rate and would hyperventilate an adult, and forceful or full-bag squeezes drive air into the stomach. One every 10 seconds is too slow and produces an inadequate minute volume.

questions.q: You are ventilating an apneic 4-year-old who has a strong pulse of 110. The correct ventilation rate is:
choices: 1 breath every 6 to 8 seconds
1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds
1 breath every 10 seconds
2 breaths back to back every 5 seconds
questions.why: For an infant or child with a pulse, rescue breathing is 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds, which is 20 to 30 breaths per minute. One breath every 6 seconds is the adult rate and would badly underventilate a child, whose oxygen demand is proportionally higher. Each breath is still delivered over about one second to visible chest rise only.

questions.q: Which bag-valve-mask technique generally results in the BEST tidal volume delivery?
choices: One rescuer using a one-handed C-E grip while squeezing the bag
Two rescuers alternating single-handed mask holds every few breaths
One rescuer squeezing the bag against the thigh for extra volume
Two rescuers, one holding the mask with two hands using a C-E grip while the other squeezes
questions.why: Two-rescuer BVM is superior because one provider can devote both hands to the mask seal using a C-E grip on each side while the second delivers the squeeze. Single-rescuer technique very commonly leaks at the mask, which is the leading cause of inadequate ventilation. Squeezing the bag against a thigh delivers excessive volume and causes gastric distension.

questions.q: During CPR on an adult with a supraglottic advanced airway in place, ventilations should be delivered:
choices: At 30 compressions to 2 breaths with pauses
Continuously, as fast as the bag can be squeezed
At 1 breath every 6 seconds without pausing compressions
At 1 breath every 3 seconds with a pause for each breath
questions.why: Once an advanced airway is placed, compressions become continuous and ventilations are given at 1 every 6 seconds, which is 10 per minute. Pausing for 30 to 2 is the technique before an advanced airway is in. Faster rates raise intrathoracic pressure, reduce venous return, and lower coronary perfusion during arrest.

questions.q: While bagging an apneic patient, you notice progressive abdominal distension and rising resistance. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: Developing tension pneumothorax from correct volumes
Ventilating too fast and with too much volume
The reservoir bag is not attached
The oxygen flow rate is set too low
questions.why: Gastric distension results from ventilating too rapidly or with too much pressure and volume, forcing air past the esophageal opening. A missing reservoir or low flow affects oxygen concentration, not stomach inflation. The distended stomach then pushes on the diaphragm and greatly increases the risk of vomiting and aspiration, so slow down and ventilate only to visible chest rise.

questions.q: Hyperventilating a patient in cardiac arrest is harmful PRIMARILY because it:
choices: Increases intrathoracic pressure and decreases venous return to the heart
Causes the patient to retain too much carbon dioxide
Increases the risk of pulmonary embolism
Raises the seizure threshold dangerously
questions.why: Excessive ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and therefore cardiac output and coronary perfusion pressure during CPR. Hyperventilation blows off CO2 rather than retaining it, so that choice is backwards. There is no link to pulmonary embolism, and the seizure concern is unrelated.

questions.q: A 68-year-old woman with a history of heart failure has crackles, pink frothy sputum, severe dyspnea, a blood pressure of 158/94, and is alert. Which intervention is MOST appropriate?
choices: Oral fluids and a position of comfort
Immediate abdominal thrusts
Continuous positive airway pressure, if within your scope
Nasal cannula at 1 L/min and transport without reassessment
questions.why: CPAP is indicated for acute pulmonary edema in an alert, hypertensive patient who can follow commands, because the positive pressure drives fluid out of the alveoli and reduces work of breathing. Abdominal thrusts treat foreign body obstruction, not fluid, and a 1 L/min cannula is grossly inadequate for this degree of distress. Oral fluids risk aspiration in a severely dyspneic patient.

questions.q: Which of the following is a CONTRAINDICATION to applying CPAP?
choices: An alert patient with pulmonary edema and crackles
A COPD patient in moderate distress who follows commands
A patient with a systolic blood pressure of 150 mmHg
A hypotensive patient with an altered mental status who is vomiting
questions.why: Hypotension, altered mental status, active vomiting, and suspected pneumothorax are all contraindications to CPAP, and this patient has three of them. Pulmonary edema and COPD are the two classic indications. A systolic pressure of 150 is reassuring, because CPAP can lower preload and worsen an already low pressure.

questions.q: CPAP for prehospital use is typically delivered at what range of pressure?
choices: 5 to 10 cm H2O
15 to 20 cm H2O
1 to 3 cm H2O
25 to 30 cm H2O
questions.why: Prehospital CPAP is usually set at about 5 to 10 cm H2O, which improves oxygenation and reduces work of breathing without excessive risk of barotrauma. Pressures of 15 to 30 cm H2O greatly increase the risk of pneumothorax and hypotension. One to 3 cm H2O is too low to recruit collapsed alveoli.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man at dinner suddenly grabs his throat. He is coughing forcefully and can speak in a hoarse voice. What is the BEST action?
choices: Perform abdominal thrusts immediately
Encourage him to keep coughing and monitor closely
Perform a blind finger sweep of the mouth
Lay him supine and begin chest compressions
questions.why: Forceful coughing and the ability to speak indicate a mild obstruction, and a patient's own cough is more effective than any maneuver you can perform. Abdominal thrusts are reserved for severe obstruction, marked by inability to speak, a silent cough, or stridor. Blind finger sweeps can drive the object deeper, and compressions are not indicated in a conscious, perfusing patient.

questions.q: A conscious adult with a severe airway obstruction suddenly becomes unresponsive. What is the NEXT action?
choices: Continue abdominal thrusts on the floor
Check for a pulse for 30 seconds before doing anything
Lower him to the ground and begin chest compressions
Perform five back slaps and five abdominal thrusts
questions.why: When a choking adult becomes unresponsive, you lower him to the ground and begin CPR starting with compressions, which generate airway pressure that may expel the object. Before each set of ventilations you open the airway and look in the mouth, removing an object only if you see it. Abdominal thrusts are not performed on an unresponsive patient, and a prolonged pulse check delays lifesaving compressions.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant is choking, cannot speak, and is turning cyanotic. Which maneuver is MOST appropriate?
choices: Abdominal thrusts just above the umbilicus
Blind finger sweeps of the oropharynx
Back blows while she lies supine
Chest thrusts at the center of the sternum
questions.why: In a patient in late pregnancy or with marked obesity, the gravid uterus or body habitus makes abdominal thrusts impractical and unsafe, so chest thrusts over the mid-sternum are used instead. Abdominal thrusts risk injury to the uterus and fetus. Back blows are not performed supine in an adult, and blind sweeps risk pushing the object deeper.

questions.q: A 7-month-old infant is choking on a grape, cannot cry, and is cyanotic. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Five abdominal thrusts, then five back slaps
Five back slaps followed by five chest thrusts, repeated
Abdominal thrusts only, using two fingers
Blind finger sweep followed by two rescue breaths
questions.why: For a responsive infant with a severe obstruction, deliver 5 back slaps with the infant face-down and head lower than the trunk, then turn and give 5 chest thrusts, repeating until the object clears or the infant becomes unresponsive. Abdominal thrusts are never used in infants because of the risk of liver and spleen injury. Blind finger sweeps can force the object deeper into a very small airway.

questions.q: A pulse oximeter reads 99 percent on an unresponsive man found in a running car in a closed garage. Which statement is MOST accurate?
choices: The reading may be falsely high because the device cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin
The reading is reliable and oxygen is unnecessary
The reading proves ventilation is adequate
Carbon monoxide causes falsely low pulse oximetry readings
questions.why: Standard pulse oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as though it were oxyhemoglobin, producing a falsely reassuring high number in carbon monoxide poisoning. This patient needs high-concentration oxygen despite the reading. Oximetry also says nothing about ventilation or CO2 clearance, which is what capnography measures.

questions.q: Which of the following would MOST likely cause an inaccurate or absent pulse oximetry reading?
choices: A warm, well-perfused hand in a calm patient
A blood pressure of 124/78 mmHg
A respiratory rate of 16 per minute
Cold extremities, poor perfusion, or dark nail polish
questions.why: Pulse oximetry depends on pulsatile arterial flow through the probe site, so hypoperfusion, hypothermia, cold fingers, nail polish, and severe anemia all degrade the signal. A warm, well-perfused hand is the ideal condition for an accurate reading. Normal vital signs do not interfere with the device. Always treat the patient's presentation, not the number alone.

questions.q: A normal end-tidal carbon dioxide reading in a healthy adult is approximately:
choices: 15 to 25 mmHg
50 to 60 mmHg
35 to 45 mmHg
60 to 80 mmHg
questions.why: Normal ETCO2 is 35 to 45 mmHg. A value in the teens or twenties suggests hyperventilation or poor pulmonary perfusion, as seen in low cardiac output states, and values above 45 suggest hypoventilation or CO2 retention. Capnography reflects ventilation and perfusion, which pulse oximetry cannot assess.

questions.q: A 25-year-old with asthma has audible expiratory wheezing, is alert, and carries a prescribed albuterol metered-dose inhaler. After obtaining medical direction, what is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Withhold the inhaler until arrival at the hospital
Coach her to exhale, actuate the inhaler while she inhales deeply, then hold her breath 5 to 10 seconds
Have her take ten rapid puffs in a row
Administer the inhaler while she exhales forcefully
questions.why: Correct MDI technique is to have the patient exhale, actuate the device at the start of a slow deep inhalation, then hold the breath for several seconds to let the medication deposit in the airways. Actuating on exhalation wastes the dose into the room. Rapid repeated puffs cause tachycardia and tremor without added benefit, and withholding a prescribed bronchodilator from a wheezing patient delays needed treatment.

questions.q: A small-volume nebulizer treatment for bronchospasm commonly uses which dose of albuterol?
choices: 2.5 mg in 3 mL of normal saline
0.3 mg in 1 mL of normal saline
10 mg in 5 mL of sterile water
0.5 mg in 10 mL of dextrose
questions.why: The standard nebulized albuterol dose is 2.5 mg in 3 mL of normal saline, driven by oxygen at roughly 6 to 8 L/min until the medication is gone. The 0.3 mg figure is an epinephrine dose and 10 mg is far above a single treatment. Nebulizers are preferred over an inhaler when the patient is too short of breath to coordinate a deep held breath.

questions.q: A 19-year-old develops hives, facial swelling, and stridor minutes after eating shrimp. The MOST important intervention is:
choices: Albuterol by nebulizer alone
An oral antihistamine and transport
Intramuscular epinephrine, plus high-concentration oxygen
CPAP at 10 cm H2O
questions.why: Stridor and facial swelling in anaphylaxis indicate upper airway edema, and epinephrine given intramuscularly in the lateral thigh is the only intervention that reverses it. Albuterol may help lower-airway bronchospasm but does nothing for laryngeal swelling. Oral antihistamines act far too slowly, and CPAP cannot force open a swollen glottis and may be contraindicated.

questions.q: A 2-year-old has a barking, seal-like cough and inspiratory stridor that worsened overnight. He is alert with mild retractions. The MOST appropriate management includes:
choices: Inspecting the pharynx with a tongue blade
Inserting an oropharyngeal airway
Immediate abdominal thrusts to relieve obstruction
Keeping the child calm, giving humidified or blow-by oxygen, and transporting
questions.why: This is croup, a viral subglottic swelling, and the mainstays are keeping the child calm, providing humidified or blow-by oxygen, and transporting in a position of comfort, often in a caregiver's arms. Agitation increases turbulent flow and worsens the stridor. There is no foreign body to thrust out, and an OPA in an alert child will provoke gagging and distress.

questions.q: A 5-year-old sits leaning forward with her chin thrust out, drooling, febrile, and with muffled voice and stridor. Which action is MOST appropriate?
choices: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Avoid putting anything in the mouth, give blow-by oxygen, and transport gently
Lay her flat and insert a nasopharyngeal airway
Perform five back blows and five abdominal thrusts
questions.why: This presentation suggests epiglottitis, and any manipulation of the oropharynx can trigger complete laryngospasm and total obstruction. Keep the child upright and calm, offer blow-by oxygen, minimize stimulation, and transport with the ability to ventilate. Laying her flat removes the position that is keeping her airway open, and thrusts are for foreign body obstruction, which this is not.

questions.q: A 5-month-old has a two-day history of cough and congestion, now with wheezing, nasal flaring, and a rate of 62. Which statement about this patient is MOST accurate?
choices: Bronchiolitis is likely, and clearing the nares is important because infants this age are obligate nose breathers
Adjuncts are unnecessary because infants breathe primarily through the mouth
A respiratory rate of 62 is normal for this age
Abdominal thrusts should be attempted to clear the wheezing
questions.why: Bronchiolitis, commonly from RSV, causes small-airway inflammation, and infants under about 6 months are obligate nose breathers, so suctioning secretions from the nares can dramatically improve their work of breathing. A rate of 62 is well above the normal infant range of 25 to 50 and reflects significant distress. Thrusts are for foreign body obstruction, not for an inflammatory lower airway process.

questions.q: Which set of normal resting respiratory rates is correct?
choices: Adult 8 to 12, child 12 to 20, infant 15 to 30
Adult 12 to 20, child 25 to 50, infant 60 to 80
Adult 20 to 30, child 25 to 50, infant 40 to 60
Adult 12 to 20, child 15 to 30, infant 25 to 50
questions.why: Normal resting rates are 12 to 20 for adults, 15 to 30 for children, and 25 to 50 for infants. Rates get faster as patients get smaller, so any answer that gives an adult a faster normal rate than an infant is reversed. An adult rate below 12 or above 20 warrants a careful look at depth and effort.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key anatomical difference in the pediatric airway compared to the adult airway?
choices: The tongue is proportionally smaller relative to the oropharynx
The trachea is more rigid and resists kinking
The narrowest point in a young child is at the level of the cricoid cartilage
The epiglottis is stiffer and less likely to obstruct
questions.why: In young children the narrowest portion of the airway is at the cricoid ring, and the tongue is proportionally larger, the trachea softer and easier to kink, and the epiglottis floppier. Each of the other options reverses a real difference. These features mean small amounts of swelling or slight overextension of the neck cause disproportionate obstruction.

questions.q: When positioning the airway of an unresponsive 8-month-old with no suspected trauma, the BEST technique is to:
choices: Place the head in a neutral sniffing position, padding under the shoulders if needed
Hyperextend the neck to maximize the opening
Place a folded towel under the occiput to flex the neck
Turn the head fully to one side
questions.why: An infant's large occiput already flexes the neck when supine, so padding goes under the shoulders and torso to bring the head to a neutral sniffing position. Hyperextension kinks the soft trachea and obstructs it, and padding under the head worsens the existing flexion. Turning the head to the side does not open the airway and may compromise it.

questions.q: Which combination of findings in a toddler indicates SEVERE respiratory distress requiring immediate intervention?
choices: Occasional cough with a clear cry and pink skin
Nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, grunting, and head bobbing
Mild rhinorrhea with a rate of 24
Playing quietly with a rate of 28
questions.why: Flaring, retractions, grunting, and head bobbing together are hallmarks of severe increased work of breathing and impending failure in a small child. Grunting in particular is an attempt to generate positive end-expiratory pressure and is an ominous sign. The other options describe children who are moving air adequately with normal or near-normal rates.

questions.q: Seesaw breathing in an infant, where the chest retracts as the abdomen rises, indicates:
choices: Normal diaphragmatic breathing for this age
Adequate tidal volume with good compliance
Ineffective ventilation and impending respiratory failure
A mild upper respiratory infection
questions.why: Seesaw or paradoxical breathing means the chest and abdomen are moving in opposite directions, indicating the infant is using the diaphragm against significant resistance and is tiring. It produces very little effective tidal volume and signals impending failure requiring assisted ventilation. It should never be mistaken for the normal belly breathing infants do, which moves chest and abdomen together.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman is breathing 30 times per minute with very shallow chest movement and is becoming confused. What is the BEST action?
choices: Apply a non-rebreather at 15 L/min and monitor
Withhold ventilation because she is still breathing on her own
Coach her to slow her breathing and have her breathe into a paper bag
Assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask, timing your breaths with her own inspiratory effort
questions.why: Fast and shallow breathing moves mostly dead-space air, so minute volume is inadequate despite the high rate, and assisted ventilation is required. Breaths are timed with the beginning of the patient's own inhalation so you do not fight her effort. A non-rebreather delivers oxygen she cannot move into the alveoli, and paper-bag rebreathing is an obsolete and dangerous practice.

questions.q: When assisting ventilations in a conscious patient who is breathing inadequately, ventilations should be:
choices: Delivered whenever you are ready, regardless of the patient's effort
Synchronized with the start of the patient's own inhalation, gradually adjusting to a normal rate
Given only during the patient's exhalation
Delivered as forcefully as possible to overcome resistance
questions.why: Squeezing at the beginning of the patient's own inhalation allows the assisted breath to augment rather than fight the patient's effort, improving volume and tolerance. Bagging during exhalation or out of sync raises airway pressure, causes gastric insufflation, and makes an anxious patient fight the mask. Force is never the answer; ventilate only to visible chest rise.

questions.q: A patient with a permanent tracheostomy stoma requires ventilation. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
choices: Attach the bag-valve mask directly to the tracheostomy tube or use an infant mask sealed over the stoma
Seal the stoma and ventilate through the mouth and nose
Insert an oropharyngeal airway and ventilate through the mouth
Perform a head-tilt, chin-lift and ventilate normally
questions.why: A patient with a permanent stoma breathes through the neck, so the BVM connects directly to the tracheostomy tube or a pediatric or infant mask is sealed over the stoma to ventilate. Ventilating through the mouth and nose will not reach the lungs in a total laryngectomy. Head positioning and oral adjuncts are irrelevant because the upper airway is no longer connected to the trachea.

questions.q: A tracheostomy patient becomes dyspneic with noisy, gurgling airflow through the tube. What is the FIRST action?
choices: Remove the tracheostomy tube entirely
Cover the stoma and apply a non-rebreather to the face
Instill sterile water and leave it in place
Suction the tube with a sterile soft catheter, applying suction on withdrawal
questions.why: A mucus plug or secretions in the tube is the most common cause of distress in a tracheostomy patient, and suctioning with a sterile soft catheter, applying vacuum only on the way out, usually resolves it. Removing the tube is beyond routine EMT practice and risks losing the airway. Covering the stoma blocks the patient's only route of breathing.

questions.q: A 62-year-old smoker with COPD has a barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing, and prolonged expiration. The pursed-lip breathing serves to:
choices: Increase carbon dioxide retention deliberately
Decrease tidal volume to conserve energy
Create back pressure that keeps small airways open during exhalation
Warm the inhaled air before it reaches the alveoli
questions.why: Pursed-lip breathing generates positive pressure during exhalation that splints collapsible small airways open, allowing more complete emptying of trapped air. It does not intentionally retain CO2, and it increases rather than decreases effective exhaled volume. Do not instruct a COPD patient to stop doing it; it is an effective compensatory mechanism.

questions.q: A 20-year-old college student is anxious after an argument, breathing 34 times per minute, and reports numb, tingling fingers and lips with carpal spasm. The MOST appropriate management is:
choices: Coach slow breathing, provide reassurance, apply oxygen as needed, and transport
Have the patient rebreathe into a paper bag until symptoms resolve
Assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask
Withhold all oxygen and restrain the patient
questions.why: Hyperventilation syndrome is treated with calm coaching, reassurance, and oxygen if the saturation warrants it, with transport because serious causes such as pulmonary embolism, diabetic ketoacidosis, and aspirin overdose can look identical. Paper-bag rebreathing is no longer recommended and has caused deaths when the true cause was hypoxic. Positive pressure ventilation is unnecessary in a patient moving large volumes on her own.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman has sudden pleuritic chest pain and severe dyspnea three days after knee surgery. Her lungs are clear and SpO2 is 89 percent. The MOST likely cause is:
choices: Acute asthma exacerbation
Pulmonary embolism
Pneumonia
Hyperventilation syndrome
questions.why: Sudden dyspnea and pleuritic pain with clear lung sounds and hypoxia after recent surgery and immobility strongly suggest pulmonary embolism, a ventilation-perfusion mismatch in which air reaches alveoli that have no blood flow. Asthma produces wheezing and pneumonia produces fever with focal crackles. Hyperventilation syndrome does not cause true hypoxia, so a saturation of 89 percent rules it out.

questions.q: A tall, thin 22-year-old man develops sudden sharp chest pain and shortness of breath while lifting. Breath sounds are absent on the right. The MOST likely condition is:
choices: Bronchiolitis
Acute pulmonary edema
Spontaneous pneumothorax
Epiglottitis
questions.why: Sudden onset of unilateral chest pain with diminished or absent breath sounds on one side in a tall, thin young man is the classic presentation of spontaneous pneumothorax from a ruptured bleb. Pulmonary edema causes bilateral crackles rather than one silent side. Bronchiolitis and epiglottitis are pediatric conditions with entirely different presentations.

questions.q: An 80-year-old nursing home resident has a productive cough, fever of 102.4 F, and crackles isolated to the right lower lobe. The MOST likely condition is:
choices: Pulmonary embolism
Spontaneous pneumothorax
Congestive heart failure
Pneumonia
questions.why: Fever, productive cough, and focal unilateral crackles point to pneumonia, an infection that fills alveoli with pus and fluid and impairs diffusion. Heart failure produces bilateral crackles with dependent edema and typically no fever. Pulmonary embolism usually leaves lungs clear and pneumothorax causes absent rather than focal adventitious sounds.

questions.q: Gas exchange between the alveoli and pulmonary capillaries occurs by which process?
choices: Diffusion from an area of higher concentration to lower concentration
Active transport across the alveolar wall
Osmosis of oxygen through the capillary membrane
Filtration driven by pulmonary artery pressure
questions.why: Oxygen and carbon dioxide move across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane by passive diffusion, each traveling down its own concentration gradient without energy expenditure. Active transport requires energy and is not how respiratory gases move. Osmosis refers specifically to water movement, and filtration describes fluid pushed across a membrane by pressure, which is not gas exchange.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST indicates that your bag-valve-mask ventilations are effective?
choices: The bag empties completely with each squeeze
You hear air escaping around the mask
Visible chest rise with each ventilation and improving skin color
The patient's abdomen distends with each breath
questions.why: Visible chest rise with each breath, along with improving color and saturation, is the primary sign that air is reaching the lungs. A mask leak means much of the volume is going into the room, and abdominal distension means it is going into the stomach. Emptying the bag fully delivers excessive volume and is not a measure of effectiveness.

questions.q: You are alone with an unresponsive adult who requires ventilation, and your mask seal keeps leaking at the bridge of the nose. What is the BEST corrective action?
choices: Increase the oxygen flow rate to 25 L/min
Reposition using a proper C-E grip and have your partner take over the seal with two hands
Squeeze the bag harder and faster
Remove the mask and ventilate mouth to mouth
questions.why: The fix for a leak is a better seal, achieved with correct C-E grip positioning and, ideally, a two-rescuer technique where one provider uses both hands on the mask. Squeezing harder simply forces more air out of the leak and into the stomach. Raising the flow rate does not improve the seal, and abandoning the BVM discards a superior device and adds exposure risk.

questions.q: Which finding is the MOST reliable early indicator that a patient's breathing has become inadequate?
choices: A pulse oximetry reading of 95 percent
A pulse rate of 88 beats per minute
A blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg
Restlessness, anxiety, and altered mental status
questions.why: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to hypoxia, so restlessness, anxiety, and confusion often appear well before the saturation falls or the vital signs change. A saturation of 95 percent is within the 94 to 99 percent target and can remain normal early, and blood pressure often stays normal until late. Never wait for a number to drop before acting on a patient who looks like he is deteriorating.

questions.q: You have an unresponsive adult in cardiac arrest and only a one-way valve pocket mask available. Which statement is MOST accurate?
choices: A pocket mask cannot be used with supplemental oxygen
A pocket mask with an oxygen inlet at 15 L/min can deliver roughly 50 to 60 percent oxygen and often achieves a better seal than a one-rescuer bag-valve mask
A pocket mask delivers only 21 percent oxygen under all conditions
A pocket mask should never be used because exhaled air is unsafe
questions.why: Most pocket masks have an oxygen inlet, and at 15 L/min they deliver about 50 to 60 percent oxygen, versus roughly 16 percent from exhaled air alone. Because both hands hold the mask, a single rescuer frequently achieves a better seal with a pocket mask than with a one-handed bag-valve mask. The one-way valve protects the rescuer, so the device is both safe and effective.

questions.q: You have ventilated an apneic adult for several minutes and now feel increasing resistance with poor chest rise. What should you check FIRST?
choices: Head position, mask seal, and the airway for obstruction or secretions
The battery level on the pulse oximeter
The patient's blood glucose level
The ambient temperature in the ambulance
questions.why: When ventilation becomes difficult, run through the correctable causes in order: reposition the head, recheck the mask seal, confirm the adjunct is placed correctly, and look and suction for obstruction or secretions. These account for the overwhelming majority of field ventilation failures and are fixable in seconds. Glucose, oximeter batteries, and cabin temperature do not affect the mechanics of moving air into the chest.

questions.q: Blood returning from the body enters the right atrium, then passes through which structure on its way to the right ventricle?
choices: The mitral valve
The aortic valve
The tricuspid valve
The pulmonic valve
questions.why: Deoxygenated blood flows from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The pulmonic valve is the next valve downstream, guarding the exit of the right ventricle, so it is out of order here. The mitral and aortic valves are on the left side of the heart and handle oxygenated blood.

questions.q: Which structure normally initiates the electrical impulse that sets the heart rate in a healthy adult?
choices: The sinoatrial node in the right atrium
The atrioventricular node at the atrial septum
The bundle of His in the interventricular septum
The Purkinje fibers in the ventricular walls
questions.why: The SA node is the primary pacemaker, firing about 60 to 100 times per minute in an adult. The AV node, bundle of His, and Purkinje fibers are backup pacemakers with progressively slower intrinsic rates and only take over if the site above them fails.

questions.q: A patient has a heart rate of 80 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL. What is the cardiac output?
choices: 150 mL per minute
1,150 mL per minute
800 mL per minute
5,600 mL per minute
questions.why: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, so 80 times 70 equals 5,600 mL, or about 5.6 liters per minute. Adding the two numbers gives 150 and is a common arithmetic error. The other values do not result from any valid combination of these figures.

questions.q: The coronary arteries that supply the heart muscle itself originate from which location?
choices: The pulmonary trunk just past the pulmonic valve
The apex of the left ventricle
The right atrium near the vena cava openings
The base of the aorta just above the aortic valve
questions.why: The left and right coronary arteries branch off the aortic root immediately above the aortic valve, and they fill mainly during diastole when the ventricle relaxes. They do not arise from the pulmonary trunk, which carries deoxygenated blood, nor from any chamber directly.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man reports crushing substernal chest pressure for 20 minutes that is not relieved by rest. What is your FIRST action after scene size-up and confirming he is alert with a patent airway?
choices: Administer 324 mg of chewable aspirin immediately
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 liters per minute
Assess his vital signs and apply a pulse oximeter
Assist him with his prescribed nitroglycerin
questions.why: Before any medication you need a baseline blood pressure, pulse, and SpO2, because nitroglycerin is withheld if the systolic pressure is below 100 mmHg and oxygen is given only if SpO2 is below 94 percent or the patient is short of breath. Aspirin and nitroglycerin both follow assessment, and blanket high-flow oxygen for a normally saturated patient is no longer recommended.

questions.q: Which patient population is MOST likely to present with an acute myocardial infarction without classic crushing chest pain?
choices: Young male athletes
Middle-aged male smokers
Patients with a history of asthma
Elderly diabetic women
questions.why: Women, diabetics, and the elderly frequently have atypical presentations such as fatigue, nausea, jaw or back discomfort, or shortness of breath alone, and diabetic neuropathy can blunt pain perception entirely. Young athletes and middle-aged male smokers, when they do infarct, more often report the classic pressure. Asthma history is unrelated to atypical infarct presentation.

questions.q: In the OPQRST mnemonic used for a chest pain history, the letter P MOST commonly stands for what?
choices: Provocation and palliation, or what makes it better or worse
Pulse quality at the time of onset
Prior cardiac history of the patient
Position the patient was found in
questions.why: P stands for provocation and palliation, exploring what brings the pain on and what relieves it. Pain reproduced by palpation or movement suggests a musculoskeletal cause, while exertional pain relieved by rest suggests angina. Past history and position are gathered elsewhere in the assessment, not under P.

questions.q: What is the key difference between stable angina and an acute myocardial infarction?
choices: Angina always radiates to the left arm while infarction never does
Angina causes reversible ischemia and resolves with rest or nitroglycerin, while infarction causes tissue death
Angina occurs only in patients over the age of 65
Angina produces a higher risk of sudden death than infarction
questions.why: Stable angina is temporary oxygen supply and demand mismatch that resolves within minutes with rest or nitroglycerin and leaves no dead muscle, whereas an infarct is prolonged occlusion causing myocardial necrosis and does not resolve with rest. Radiation patterns overlap heavily between the two, angina is not age restricted, and infarction carries the higher mortality.

questions.q: Your protocol directs 324 mg of aspirin for suspected acute coronary syndrome. How is this dose usually given?
choices: One 324 mg enteric-coated tablet swallowed with water
Four 81 mg chewable tablets chewed and swallowed
Two 162 mg tablets placed under the tongue
Three 108 mg tablets dissolved in juice
questions.why: The standard EMT dose is four 81 mg chewable baby aspirin, chewed so the drug is absorbed rapidly and can inhibit platelet aggregation. Enteric-coated tablets swallowed whole dissolve too slowly to help acutely. Aspirin is not a sublingual medication, and 108 mg tablets do not exist.

questions.q: A 66-year-old woman with chest pressure tells you she gets hives and throat swelling from aspirin. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Give half the usual aspirin dose to reduce the reaction risk
Give the aspirin and be ready with oxygen if she reacts
Withhold aspirin and continue the rest of your cardiac care
Substitute her husband's prescription blood thinner
questions.why: A true allergy to aspirin is an absolute contraindication, and a documented hives and airway reaction qualifies, so the aspirin is withheld and everything else in the protocol continues. Reducing the dose does not reduce the risk of an allergic reaction, which is not dose dependent. Administering another person's prescription medication is outside EMT scope and unsafe.

questions.q: What is the usual dose and route of nitroglycerin an EMT may assist a patient in taking for chest pain?
choices: 0.4 mg sublingual, up to three doses five minutes apart
0.4 mg intramuscular, up to two doses ten minutes apart
4 mg sublingual, one dose only
0.04 mg oral tablet swallowed every fifteen minutes
questions.why: Nitroglycerin is given as 0.4 mg sublingually and may be repeated at five-minute intervals up to a total of three doses, with a blood pressure check before each dose. It is not given intramuscularly, the 4 mg figure is ten times too high, and swallowing the tablet destroys it in first-pass metabolism.

questions.q: A 54-year-old man with chest pain has a blood pressure of 88/54 mmHg and his own nitroglycerin in hand. What should you do?
choices: Assist with one dose and recheck the pressure in five minutes
Assist with a half tablet to limit the pressure drop
Have him lie flat and then assist with a full dose
Withhold the nitroglycerin and transport
questions.why: Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator and is contraindicated when the systolic pressure is below 100 mmHg, because further dilation can collapse coronary perfusion. Halving the tablet is not an accepted workaround and is not reliably dosed. Lying the patient flat does not correct the underlying hypotension, and the drug is still contraindicated.

questions.q: A 49-year-old man with substernal chest pain admits he took sildenafil about six hours ago. What is the MOST important implication?
choices: Aspirin must also be withheld because of a drug interaction
His chest pain is almost certainly non-cardiac in origin
Nitroglycerin must be withheld because of the risk of profound hypotension
He should be given two nitroglycerin doses at once to overcome the interaction
questions.why: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors like sildenafil and tadalafil combined with nitrates can cause severe refractory hypotension, so nitroglycerin is held for at least 24 hours after sildenafil and up to 48 hours after tadalafil. Aspirin has no such interaction and should still be given. Erectile dysfunction drug use does not rule out a true cardiac event, and doubling the nitrate dose would be dangerous.

questions.q: Five minutes after a first nitroglycerin dose, a chest pain patient reports a throbbing headache and feels lightheaded. What is your BEST next step?
choices: Recheck the blood pressure before considering another dose
Stop all care and request an immediate ALS rendezvous for the headache
Give a second dose right away since headache proves the drug is working
Have the patient stand up to see if the dizziness resolves
questions.why: Headache and lightheadedness are expected vasodilatory side effects, but lightheadedness may also signal hypotension, so a blood pressure must be obtained before any repeat dose. Headache alone is not a reason to abandon the chest pain protocol, giving a second dose without a pressure is unsafe, and standing a possibly hypotensive patient risks syncope.

questions.q: A chest pain patient is alert, breathing comfortably, and has an SpO2 of 97 percent on room air. What is the MOST appropriate oxygen therapy?
choices: A nonrebreather at 15 liters per minute for all chest pain
A nasal cannula at 6 liters per minute as a precaution
Bag-valve-mask ventilation to increase delivery
No supplemental oxygen at this time
questions.why: Current guidelines call for supplemental oxygen only when the SpO2 is below 94 percent or the patient is dyspneic, because routine oxygen in normoxic cardiac patients offers no benefit and may worsen outcomes. Neither a mask nor a cannula is indicated here, and assisted ventilation is reserved for inadequate breathing.

questions.q: Why is early acquisition and transmission of a 12-lead ECG valuable in a suspected acute coronary syndrome?
choices: It allows the EMT to independently diagnose and treat the blockage
It identifies STEMI early so the receiving hospital can activate the cath lab
It replaces the need for aspirin administration in the field
It reliably rules out a heart attack when it appears normal
questions.why: Prehospital 12-lead acquisition and transmission shortens first-medical-contact to balloon time by letting the hospital mobilize the PCI team before arrival. EMTs acquire and transmit but do not diagnose or treat the occlusion, aspirin is still indicated, and a single normal 12-lead never excludes an infarct.

questions.q: Your STEMI patient is 15 minutes from a community hospital without a cath lab and 40 minutes from a PCI center. What transport decision is MOST appropriate?
choices: Transport to the closest hospital because time matters most
Let the patient choose without offering guidance
Contact medical direction and transport to the PCI center per your STEMI protocol
Stay on scene and wait for a helicopter regardless of weather
questions.why: STEMI systems of care direct patients to a PCI-capable facility when the additional transport time is acceptable, generally allowing a first-contact-to-balloon time within 120 minutes, and medical direction confirms the destination. Going to the closest hospital adds a transfer delay. Deferring entirely to the patient without guidance and waiting on an unnecessary aircraft both waste critical time.

questions.q: A 77-year-old man wakes at night gasping, must sit upright to breathe, and has swollen ankles and crackles at both lung bases. What condition do these findings BEST support?
choices: Spontaneous pneumothorax
Acute asthma exacerbation
Pulmonary embolism
Congestive heart failure with pulmonary edema
questions.why: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, pedal edema, and bibasilar crackles are the classic picture of left-sided failure backing fluid into the lungs with right-sided congestion in the legs. A pneumothorax gives unilateral absent sounds, asthma gives wheezing without pedal edema, and pulmonary embolism typically gives sudden dyspnea with clear lungs.

questions.q: A patient in severe pulmonary edema is coughing pink frothy sputum, has an SpO2 of 84 percent, and is speaking in one-word sentences. Which intervention is MOST appropriate if it is within your scope and protocol?
choices: Place the patient supine and suction the airway continuously
Withhold oxygen until a blood pressure is obtained
Encourage slow deep breathing into a paper bag
Apply CPAP with the patient sitting upright
questions.why: CPAP with the patient upright drives fluid out of the alveoli, improves oxygenation, and often prevents intubation in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Lying the patient flat worsens the work of breathing dramatically. Paper bag rebreathing is for suspected hyperventilation syndrome, and hypoxia at 84 percent must be treated immediately.

questions.q: Jugular venous distention seen while a patient sits at a 45-degree angle MOST directly suggests which problem?
choices: Dehydration from prolonged vomiting
Backup of blood into the systemic venous system
Acute arterial occlusion in the neck
Hyperventilation from anxiety
questions.why: JVD reflects elevated pressure in the venous system returning to the right heart, seen in right-sided heart failure, cardiac tamponade, and tension pneumothorax. Dehydration produces flat neck veins, not distended ones. JVD is a venous finding rather than arterial, and anxiety does not distend the jugular veins.

questions.q: A patient with a recent large myocardial infarction is cool, mottled, and confused with a blood pressure of 76/50 mmHg and crackles in both lungs. Which type of shock is MOST likely?
choices: Hypovolemic shock
Anaphylactic shock
Neurogenic shock
Cardiogenic shock
questions.why: A failing pump after a large infarct produces hypotension with signs of backward congestion such as crackles and JVD, which is cardiogenic shock. Hypovolemic shock follows fluid loss and presents with dry lungs and flat neck veins, anaphylaxis involves an allergen with hives and airway swelling, and neurogenic shock produces warm dry skin with bradycardia after spinal injury.

questions.q: Which term describes the volume of blood returning to and filling the ventricle just before contraction?
choices: Afterload
Peripheral vascular resistance
Ejection fraction
Preload
questions.why: Preload is the ventricular filling volume at the end of diastole, and greater stretch within limits produces a stronger contraction. Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject, ejection fraction is the percentage of preload actually ejected, and peripheral vascular resistance is one contributor to afterload rather than filling.

questions.q: A 62-year-old woman has a blood pressure of 224/128 mmHg with a severe headache, blurred vision, and new confusion. How should this be classified and managed?
choices: Hypertensive emergency requiring calm handling and prompt transport
Normal variation in an anxious patient that needs only reassurance
An indication for the EMT to administer nitroglycerin to lower pressure
A reason to have the patient walk to the ambulance to reduce anxiety
questions.why: Severe hypertension with end-organ symptoms such as headache, visual change, and altered mental status is a hypertensive emergency that needs a quiet environment, minimal stimulation, upright positioning, and rapid transport. EMTs do not carry antihypertensives, and nitroglycerin is a chest pain medication given under specific protocol, not a blood pressure treatment. Exertion can worsen the situation.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man describes a sudden tearing pain between his shoulder blades, and you find a markedly weaker radial pulse on the left than the right. What should you suspect?
choices: Simple musculoskeletal back strain
Acute pericarditis
Aortic dissection
Pulmonary edema from heart failure
questions.why: Abrupt tearing or ripping pain radiating to the back with a pulse or blood pressure difference between the arms is the hallmark of aortic dissection, and these patients need gentle handling and rapid transport to a surgical center. A strain does not cause a pulse deficit, pericarditis pain typically worsens lying flat and improves leaning forward, and pulmonary edema presents with dyspnea and crackles.

questions.q: You find an unresponsive adult who is making occasional slow gasping sounds. What is the MOST appropriate interpretation?
choices: He is breathing adequately, so monitor and give oxygen
These are agonal gasps and do not count as normal breathing
He is snoring, so a head tilt will resolve the situation
He is hyperventilating and needs coaching to slow down
questions.why: Agonal gasps are an abnormal brainstem reflex common in the first minutes of cardiac arrest and must not be mistaken for breathing, so you check for a pulse for no more than 10 seconds and begin CPR if absent. Treating gasps as adequate breathing is a leading cause of delayed CPR. Snoring implies airway obstruction in a patient who is actually ventilating, and hyperventilation is fast, not slow and gasping.

questions.q: How long should you spend checking for a carotid pulse in an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally?
choices: No more than 10 seconds
At least 30 seconds to be certain
A full 60 seconds before starting CPR
Until an ALS unit arrives to confirm
questions.why: The pulse check is limited to 10 seconds because prolonged checks delay compressions and because pulse detection is unreliable even for experienced providers. If no definite pulse is felt within 10 seconds, compressions begin immediately. Waiting 30 or 60 seconds, or deferring to ALS, costs perfusion time that directly lowers survival.

questions.q: What are the correct rate and depth for chest compressions on an adult in cardiac arrest?
choices: 60 to 80 per minute at a depth of 1 inch
100 to 120 per minute at a depth of at least 2 inches but not more than 2.4 inches
80 to 100 per minute at a depth of 3 inches
140 to 160 per minute at a depth of 1.5 inches
questions.why: AHA guidelines specify 100 to 120 compressions per minute with a depth of at least 2 inches and not exceeding 2.4 inches in an average adult. Slower or shallower compressions fail to generate coronary perfusion pressure, and excessive rate or depth reduces filling and increases injury.

questions.q: Why is complete chest recoil between compressions important during CPR?
choices: It prevents rib fractures from occurring
It keeps the AED pads from losing adhesion
It reduces the amount of oxygen the rescuer consumes
It allows the heart to refill, improving the output of the next compression
questions.why: Full recoil creates the negative intrathoracic pressure that draws blood back into the heart, so leaning on the chest directly reduces cardiac output and coronary perfusion. Recoil does not prevent rib fractures, has nothing to do with rescuer oxygen consumption, and does not affect pad adhesion.

questions.q: During two-rescuer adult CPR without an advanced airway, what compression-to-ventilation ratio should be used?
choices: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
Continuous compressions with no breaths at all
5 compressions to 1 breath
30 compressions to 2 breaths
questions.why: Adults receive 30 compressions to 2 breaths whether there are one or two rescuers without an advanced airway. The 15 to 2 ratio applies only to children and infants with two rescuers. The 5 to 1 ratio is obsolete, and compression-only CPR is the layperson option, not the standard for trained EMTs with a BVM.

questions.q: Once an advanced airway such as a supraglottic device is in place during adult CPR, how should ventilations be delivered?
choices: Pause compressions every 30 compressions for 2 breaths
Squeeze the bag as fast as possible to maximize oxygen
One breath every 6 seconds with continuous compressions
One breath every 2 seconds to correct the acidosis
questions.why: With an advanced airway, compressions become continuous and ventilations are given at one breath every 6 seconds, about 10 per minute. Cycling back to 30 to 2 needlessly interrupts compressions. Rapid or excessive ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return, and worsens survival.

questions.q: What is the MAIN reason rescuers should switch compressor roles about every 2 minutes?
choices: Rescuer fatigue degrades compression depth and rate before the rescuer notices
It gives each rescuer a chance to reassess the patient history
Guidelines require rotating so each rescuer gets equal documentation credit
Switching allows the AED battery to cool between analyses
questions.why: Compression quality measurably declines within one to two minutes even though the rescuer usually still feels fine, so a scheduled swap during the rhythm analysis preserves depth and rate. The swap is not for history taking or documentation, and AED batteries do not require a cooling period.

questions.q: Chest compression fraction is a quality measure of resuscitation. What target should a team aim for?
choices: Above 30 percent
Above 45 percent
Above 60 percent
Exactly 100 percent with no pauses at all
questions.why: Compression fraction is the proportion of the arrest time spent actually compressing, and the goal is greater than 60 percent, with higher being better. Values of 30 or 45 percent reflect excessive interruptions. A literal 100 percent is impossible because brief pauses for defibrillation and rhythm checks are still necessary.

questions.q: Interruptions in chest compressions during a resuscitation should be limited to what maximum duration?
choices: Less than 30 seconds
Less than 20 seconds
Less than 10 seconds
Less than 60 seconds if the team is switching roles
questions.why: Any pause should be held under 10 seconds because coronary perfusion pressure falls quickly and takes many compressions to rebuild. Longer pauses of 20, 30, or 60 seconds substantially reduce the chance of successful defibrillation, and a compressor swap should be completed within that same 10-second window during rhythm analysis.

questions.q: An AED advises a shock on an adult in cardiac arrest and you deliver it. What should happen IMMEDIATELY next?
choices: Resume chest compressions without checking a pulse
Check for a carotid pulse for 10 seconds
Reanalyze the rhythm right away to confirm conversion
Ventilate with 5 rescue breaths before touching the chest
questions.why: Compressions resume immediately after the shock because a perfusing rhythm rarely returns instantly and any pulse check wastes critical seconds. The rhythm is reanalyzed after the next 2 minutes of CPR, not right after the shock. Delivering a burst of breaths first also delays compressions unnecessarily.

questions.q: Which pair of rhythms is shockable with an AED?
choices: Asystole and pulseless electrical activity
Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia
Sinus bradycardia and first-degree AV block
Atrial fibrillation with a pulse and sinus tachycardia
questions.why: Only ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are shockable, because defibrillation depolarizes chaotic ventricular activity so the SA node can resume. Asystole and PEA have no disorganized ventricular activity to stop, so shocking them provides no benefit and interrupts compressions. Perfusing rhythms are never defibrillated with an AED.

questions.q: A partner insists on shocking a flat-line asystolic patient because he believes it will restart the heart. What is the BEST response?
choices: Agree, since a single shock is harmless and might help
Shock only if the patient has been down less than five minutes
Defibrillate at a lower energy setting as a compromise
Explain that asystole is not shockable and continue high-quality CPR
questions.why: Asystole represents the absence of electrical activity, so defibrillation cannot organize anything and the pause only reduces perfusion. High-quality compressions with attention to reversible causes is the correct treatment. Down time and energy level do not change the fact that the rhythm is non-shockable, and an AED will not advise a shock for it anyway.

questions.q: Pulseless electrical activity is BEST described as which of the following?
choices: An organized rhythm on the monitor with no palpable pulse
Complete absence of electrical activity with occasional gasps
A rapid ventricular rhythm that always converts with a single shock
A normal pulse with an abnormal-looking electrical tracing
questions.why: In PEA the monitor shows organized electrical complexes but the heart is not generating effective mechanical output, so no pulse is felt. Absent electrical activity is asystole. PEA is non-shockable, and the definition requires an absent pulse, not a normal one, so treatment is CPR and correcting reversible causes.

questions.q: You are preparing to apply AED pads to a man with a hairy chest that is wet from sweat. What is the BEST preparation?
choices: Dry the chest and shave the pad sites if the pads will not adhere
Apply the pads over the hair and press hard to compensate
Pour water on the chest to improve conduction
Place both pads on the abdomen where there is less hair
questions.why: Poor pad contact from moisture or hair causes impedance, ineffective shocks, and burns, so the chest is briskly dried and the sites shaved with the razor in the AED kit. Pressing pads onto hair does not create skin contact, adding water creates an arcing path across the skin, and abdominal placement does not put the current across the heart.

questions.q: You notice a hard implanted pacemaker bulge under the skin where you planned to place an AED pad. What should you do?
choices: Withhold defibrillation entirely because of the device
Place the pad directly over the device for best contact
Position the pad at least 1 inch away from the implanted device
Remove the device before applying the pad
questions.why: Pads are placed at least 1 inch from an implanted pacemaker or defibrillator so the current is not shunted through the generator, which can damage the device and waste energy on the heart. Defibrillation is still absolutely indicated in a shockable arrest, and no EMT ever removes an implanted device.

questions.q: An adult arrest patient has a nitroglycerin transdermal patch on the left upper chest where a pad belongs. What is the correct action?
choices: Leave the patch in place and shift the pad slightly lower
Remove the patch with a gloved hand, wipe the skin, then apply the pad
Shock through the patch since the medication is not flammable
Cut a hole in the patch and apply the pad through the opening
questions.why: Medication patches are removed with a gloved hand and the residue wiped off, because shocking through a patch can cause arcing, skin burns, and reduced energy delivery to the heart. Leaving the patch in place, shocking through it, or cutting it all keep conductive backing and residue in the current path.

questions.q: You are treating a 5-year-old, about 20 kg, in cardiac arrest and the AED has both adult and pediatric pads. Which should you use?
choices: Adult pads, because they cover more surface area
Pediatric pads or a dose attenuator
Either type, since energy is identical
No pads at all, because AEDs are contraindicated under age 8
questions.why: Children under 8 years or under 25 kg should receive pediatric pads or an attenuator that reduces the delivered energy to a weight-appropriate dose. AEDs are indicated in pediatric arrest, not contraindicated, and the pad types do not deliver the same energy. If only adult pads are available they should be used rather than withholding defibrillation.

questions.q: Only pediatric AED pads are available for an adult in ventricular fibrillation. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Apply the pediatric pads and deliver the reduced-energy shock
Apply two sets of pediatric pads to double the energy
Do not use the pediatric pads on an adult and continue CPR while awaiting an adult-capable defibrillator
Delay CPR until the correct pads arrive
questions.why: Pediatric pads deliver an attenuated energy dose that is too low to reliably defibrillate an adult heart, so they should not be substituted; the team continues high-quality CPR until an adult-capable device arrives. Stacking pads is not a valid technique, and CPR is never delayed while waiting for equipment.

questions.q: During an ongoing resuscitation with an AED attached, how often should the rhythm be analyzed?
choices: Every 30 seconds
Every 2 minutes
Every 5 minutes
Only when the patient appears to move
questions.why: The AED analyzes every 2 minutes, which coincides neatly with the compressor change and keeps interruptions infrequent. Analyzing every 30 seconds destroys compression fraction, waiting 5 minutes delays the detection of a shockable rhythm, and waiting for movement is not a reliable trigger.

questions.q: An unwitnessed adult collapse is found by your crew with an AED already on scene. What is the recommended sequence?
choices: Give 2 minutes of CPR first, then attach the AED
Attach and use the AED as soon as it is available while CPR continues
Attach the AED only after ALS arrives
Give 5 rescue breaths before any compressions or AED use
questions.why: Current guidelines direct that the AED be applied as soon as it is available, with compressions continuing while the pads go on, because early defibrillation is the strongest predictor of survival in a shockable rhythm. The older routine of 2 minutes of CPR before analysis is no longer recommended, and neither waiting for ALS nor beginning with rescue breaths applies to adult sudden collapse.

questions.q: You pull an unresponsive, pulseless teenager from a lake. How does the initial approach differ from a standard adult sudden collapse?
choices: Start with about 2 minutes of rescue breaths and CPR because the arrest is hypoxic in origin
Withhold all compressions until the patient is fully dry
Perform abdominal thrusts first to clear water from the lungs
Use only compressions and no ventilations at all
questions.why: Drowning arrest is caused by hypoxia, so ventilations are a priority and rescue breathing with CPR begins promptly rather than defaulting to compression-only care. Compressions are not delayed for drying, though the chest is dried before pads are applied. Abdominal thrusts to expel water are not recommended and risk aspiration of stomach contents.

questions.q: A hiker is found cold, stiff, and pulseless after prolonged exposure with a core temperature well below normal. Which principle applies?
choices: Resuscitation is futile once the skin is cold to the touch
Hypothermic patients should be rewarmed before CPR is started
CPR should be performed with vigorous rough handling to generate heat
Prolonged resuscitation with careful handling is warranted because hypothermia is protective
questions.why: Hypothermia lowers metabolic demand and can protect the brain, so resuscitation continues during rewarming and the patient is not declared dead until warm and dead. Cold skin alone does not establish futility. CPR is never delayed for rewarming, and rough handling of a cold heart can precipitate ventricular fibrillation.

questions.q: A 26-year-old is unresponsive and pulseless next to a syringe, with pinpoint pupils. What is the priority?
choices: Administer naloxone first and reassess before starting CPR
Begin high-quality CPR and give naloxone when it does not interrupt resuscitation
Apply the AED and shock regardless of the displayed rhythm
Withhold naloxone entirely because it is not useful in cardiac arrest
questions.why: In confirmed cardiac arrest, high-quality CPR and defibrillation for shockable rhythms are the priority, with naloxone given as an adjunct that must not delay compressions. Giving naloxone first delays perfusion. Shocking a non-shockable rhythm is harmful, and naloxone is still reasonable in suspected opioid arrest rather than forbidden.

questions.q: A woman who appears about 34 weeks pregnant is in cardiac arrest. Which modification should be used during CPR?
choices: Compress the lower sternum to avoid the uterus
Perform manual left uterine displacement while compressing
Place the patient fully prone to relieve caval compression
Reduce compression depth to about 1 inch to protect the fetus
questions.why: In late pregnancy the gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava, so a rescuer manually displaces the uterus to the patient's left to restore venous return while compressions continue on a firm flat surface. Hand position moves slightly higher on the sternum, not lower, prone positioning makes compressions impossible, and depth is not reduced.

questions.q: A trauma patient in cardiac arrest after a high-speed collision presents with no pulse. What is the MOST appropriate approach?
choices: Provide CPR while treating reversible causes such as hemorrhage and airway obstruction, and transport rapidly
Withhold all resuscitation because traumatic arrest is always fatal
Focus exclusively on splinting fractures before beginning CPR
Apply the AED and shock repeatedly regardless of rhythm
questions.why: Traumatic arrest has poor but not zero survival, and the best chance comes from controlling catastrophic hemorrhage, opening the airway, decompressing the chest when in scope, and rapid transport alongside CPR.
