Withholding care is only appropriate when injuries are incompatible with life, splinting is never a priority over perfusion, and repeated blind shocking is not indicated.

questions.q: Which finding makes it appropriate to withhold resuscitation on an apparently deceased patient?
choices: The patient appears elderly and frail
A family member states the patient did not want heroic measures
Obvious dependent lividity and rigor mortis are present
The patient has been unresponsive for about four minutes
questions.why: Definitive signs of death such as rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decapitation, decomposition, or injuries incompatible with life justify withholding resuscitation. Age and frailty are never criteria. A verbal family statement without a valid DNR or POLST generally does not meet the legal standard, and four minutes of down time is a reason to start CPR, not withhold it.

questions.q: You are handed a valid, signed POLST form specifying do not attempt resuscitation for a pulseless patient. What should you do?
choices: Begin CPR anyway because the form might be outdated
Honor the form, provide comfort measures and family support, and contact medical direction as your protocol requires
Ask the family to vote on whether to start CPR
Start CPR but stop as soon as the family objects
questions.why: A valid DNR or POLST is a legal physician order that must be honored, and the appropriate care shifts to comfort, family support, and notification per protocol. Presuming the form is outdated without evidence overrides the patient's documented wishes. Family consensus does not override a valid order, and starting then stopping based on objections is inconsistent care.

questions.q: Your crew has run a prolonged resuscitation with no return of circulation and persistent asystole. Who ordinarily authorizes termination of resuscitation in the field?
choices: The senior EMT on scene using personal judgment
A law enforcement officer at the scene
The patient's next of kin by verbal request
Online or offline medical direction under an established protocol
questions.why: Field termination requires authorization from medical direction, either through direct online contact or a written protocol with defined criteria, and the decision is documented. An EMT cannot unilaterally terminate, law enforcement has no medical authority over resuscitation, and family cannot authorize termination in the absence of a valid advance directive.

questions.q: You achieve return of spontaneous circulation on an adult. Which set of actions is MOST appropriate immediately afterward?
choices: Reassess airway and breathing, ventilate at 1 breath every 6 seconds if needed, obtain a blood pressure, and transport rapidly
Remove the AED pads and allow the patient to sit up
Hyperventilate at 20 breaths per minute to wash out carbon dioxide
Delay transport for 20 minutes to observe for rearrest on scene
questions.why: Post-ROSC care centers on reassessing the airway, providing adequate but not excessive ventilation at about 10 breaths per minute, titrating oxygen, obtaining a blood pressure since hypotension is common, and moving quickly to definitive care. Pads stay attached because rearrest is common. Hyperventilation lowers cerebral blood flow, and delaying transport offers no benefit.

questions.q: Why is closed-loop communication emphasized during a resuscitation?
choices: It shortens the written documentation required afterward
It is required only when a physician is physically present
It allows the team leader to perform compressions at the same time
It confirms that an assigned task was heard and completed, preventing missed or duplicated interventions
questions.why: Closed-loop communication means the team leader assigns a task by name, the receiver repeats it back, and reports when it is done, which prevents tasks from being dropped or done twice during a chaotic event. It is not a documentation shortcut, the team leader should stay hands-off to maintain situational awareness, and it applies to every resuscitation regardless of who is present.

questions.q: What is the correct compression depth for a 6-year-old child in cardiac arrest?
choices: About 1 inch
About 1.5 inches
About 2 inches, or one third the anterior-posterior chest diameter
At least 3 inches to ensure adequate perfusion
questions.why: Children are compressed about 2 inches or one third of the front-to-back chest depth, whichever guide is easier to apply at the bedside. About 1.5 inches is the infant depth, 1 inch is inadequate at any age, and 3 inches exceeds safe depth for a child's chest.

questions.q: You and your partner are performing CPR on a 4-month-old infant. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should you use?
choices: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
10 compressions to 1 breath
5 compressions to 1 breath
15 compressions to 2 breaths
questions.why: With two rescuers, infants and children receive 15 compressions to 2 breaths because pediatric arrest is usually hypoxic and needs more frequent ventilation. A single rescuer uses 30 to 2 for the same patient. The 5 to 1 and 10 to 1 ratios are not part of current guidelines.

questions.q: Which compression technique is preferred for a two-rescuer infant resuscitation?
choices: Heel of one hand on the lower sternum
Two thumbs with the hands encircling the chest
Both hands stacked as in an adult
Three fingers over the upper sternum
questions.why: The two-thumb encircling technique is preferred with two rescuers because it generates higher compression pressure and more consistent depth than the two-finger method used by a lone rescuer. One-hand and two-hand techniques are for children and adults, and upper sternal compression does not compress the ventricles.

questions.q: Most pediatric cardiac arrests differ from adult arrests in which important way?
choices: They are usually caused by respiratory failure or shock rather than a primary cardiac rhythm
They are almost always caused by ventricular fibrillation
They respond better to defibrillation than to ventilation
They are usually caused by coronary artery blockage
questions.why: Children most often arrest from progressive hypoxia or shock, so aggressive airway management and ventilation are central and a shockable rhythm is comparatively uncommon. Ventricular fibrillation and coronary occlusion dominate adult arrests, not pediatric ones, and defibrillation helps only the minority of pediatric cases in a shockable rhythm.

questions.q: A newborn has been dried, warmed, positioned, and stimulated, and 30 seconds later the heart rate is 84 beats per minute with weak respiratory effort. What is the NEXT action?
choices: Begin chest compressions at a 3 to 1 ratio
Provide free-flow blow-by oxygen and continue to observe
Begin positive pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths per minute
Immediately transport without further intervention
questions.why: A newborn heart rate below 100 after the initial steps calls for positive pressure ventilation, which is the single most effective intervention in neonatal resuscitation. Compressions are added only if the rate stays below 60 after 30 seconds of effective PPV. Blow-by oxygen alone does not correct inadequate ventilation, and transport without intervention abandons the treatable problem.

questions.q: After 30 seconds of effective positive pressure ventilation, a newborn's heart rate is 48 beats per minute. What should you do?
choices: Continue ventilation alone and recheck in two minutes
Start chest compressions coordinated 3 to 1 with ventilations at 120 events per minute
Start compressions at a 30 to 2 ratio as in an adult
Stop ventilation and check a blood pressure
questions.why: A newborn heart rate under 60 after adequate PPV requires chest compressions coordinated with ventilation at a 3 to 1 ratio, producing 90 compressions and 30 breaths, or 120 events, each minute. Ventilation alone at that rate is insufficient. The adult 30 to 2 ratio does not apply to newborns, and blood pressure is not a useful neonatal decision point in the field.

questions.q: Which of the following is the FIRST step in caring for a newly delivered newborn who is crying vigorously?
choices: Suction the stomach with a bulb syringe
Clamp and cut the cord immediately
Dry, warm, and position the infant while assessing
Begin positive pressure ventilation preemptively
questions.why: Drying, warming, positioning the airway, and stimulating are the universal first steps, and a vigorously crying newborn with good tone needs little else besides warmth and skin-to-skin contact. Routine deep suctioning is no longer recommended for a vigorous infant, cord management follows its own timing, and PPV is not given to a baby who is already breathing well.

questions.q: Which vital sign finding is MOST concerning in a 2-year-old with severe dehydration and tachycardia?
choices: A respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute
A heart rate of 150 beats per minute
A systolic blood pressure of 62 mmHg
A capillary refill time of 2 seconds
questions.why: Hypotension in a child is a very late and ominous finding because children compensate with tachycardia and vasoconstriction until they are near collapse, and a systolic pressure of 62 mmHg in a toddler indicates decompensated shock. A rate of 30 breaths and a heart rate of 150 are within or near normal toddler ranges, and a 2-second capillary refill is acceptable.

questions.q: An 8-month-old has a heart rate of 170, mottled skin, and delayed capillary refill, but a palpable pulse and a normal blood pressure for age. How is this BEST classified?
choices: Compensated shock
Decompensated shock
Irreversible shock
No shock, because the blood pressure is normal
questions.why: Compensated shock means perfusion is failing but the body is maintaining blood pressure through tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction, which is exactly what mottling and delayed refill with a normal pressure indicate. Decompensated shock is marked by hypotension, irreversible shock implies organ damage beyond recovery, and a normal pressure does not exclude shock in a child.

questions.q: Which type of shock results from a mechanical barrier to cardiac filling or outflow, such as a tension pneumothorax or cardiac tamponade?
choices: Distributive shock
Hypovolemic shock
Obstructive shock
Cardiogenic shock
questions.why: Obstructive shock occurs when something physically blocks filling or ejection, as with tamponade, tension pneumothorax, or massive pulmonary embolism, and the treatment is relieving the obstruction. Distributive shock is abnormal vessel dilation, hypovolemic shock is volume loss, and cardiogenic shock is intrinsic pump failure.

questions.q: Which set of interventions is MOST appropriate for an adult in compensated hypovolemic shock from internal bleeding?
choices: Give small sips of water to replace lost volume
Keep the patient supine and warm, give oxygen as indicated, keep him NPO, and transport rapidly
Have the patient sit fully upright to improve breathing
Apply cold packs to the extremities to slow the bleeding
questions.why: Shock care centers on maintaining perfusion and body temperature, supporting oxygenation, giving nothing by mouth because surgery is likely and the airway is at risk, and transporting without delay. Oral fluids risk aspiration and do not restore intravascular volume. Sitting upright worsens cerebral perfusion, and chilling the extremities promotes the hypothermia that worsens coagulopathy.

questions.q: What capillary refill time is considered normal in a warm adult or child?
choices: Less than 2 seconds
Less than 5 seconds
Less than 8 seconds
Any refill at all, regardless of time
questions.why: Capillary refill under 2 seconds indicates adequate peripheral perfusion, while delayed refill suggests vasoconstriction from shock. Times of 5 or 8 seconds represent significant perfusion failure. The finding is less reliable in cold environments or in older adults, so it is interpreted with other signs rather than in isolation.

questions.q: A 30-year-old stung by a bee is warm, flushed, and hypotensive with hives and wheezing. Which type of shock is present?
choices: Cardiogenic shock
Obstructive shock
Hypovolemic shock
Distributive shock
questions.why: Anaphylaxis is a form of distributive shock in which massive vasodilation and capillary leak drop the pressure despite a normal blood volume, which is why the skin is warm and flushed rather than cool and pale. Cardiogenic and obstructive shock produce cool clammy skin, and there has been no volume loss to make this hypovolemic.

questions.q: A 19-year-old faints briefly at a concert after standing for hours, then wakes fully oriented with normal vital signs. What is the MOST likely mechanism?
choices: Vasovagal syncope with transient cerebral hypoperfusion
An acute myocardial infarction
A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
A hypertensive emergency
questions.why: Prolonged standing with venous pooling triggers a vagal response, briefly dropping heart rate and blood pressure enough to cause loss of consciousness, with rapid full recovery once the patient is horizontal. Infarction and aneurysm rupture in a healthy 19-year-old are extremely unlikely and would not resolve spontaneously, and a hypertensive emergency involves severe hypertension, not a faint.

questions.q: A 45-year-old reports a sudden racing heartbeat with a regular pulse too fast to count, mild lightheadedness, but a blood pressure of 118/72 mmHg and clear lungs. What is the MOST appropriate EMT care?
choices: Instruct him to hold his breath and press firmly on both carotid arteries
Assist him with a neighbor's beta blocker to slow the rate
Position him comfortably, give oxygen if indicated, acquire a 12-lead if trained, monitor closely, and transport
Withhold transport since he is not hypotensive
questions.why: A stable tachycardic patient gets supportive care, monitoring, a 12-lead when available, and transport for definitive evaluation, since deterioration can occur quickly. Bilateral carotid pressure is dangerous and not an EMT maneuver. Administering another person's prescription medication is outside scope, and normal vital signs never justify refusing transport for new palpitations.

questions.q: A stabbing victim has absent breath sounds on the left, hypotension, and a rapid weak pulse without tracheal deviation. What is the MOST likely cause of his shock?
choices: Neurogenic shock from spinal injury
Septic shock from wound contamination
Psychogenic shock from fear
Massive hemothorax filling the chest with blood
questions.why: Blood accumulating in the pleural space causes both absent breath sounds and hypovolemic shock from blood loss, and unlike tension pneumothorax the neck veins are usually flat. Neurogenic shock gives warm dry skin with bradycardia, sepsis takes many hours to develop, and psychogenic shock is a transient faint rather than sustained hypotension.

questions.q: Which statement about the electrical conduction pathway is MOST accurate?
choices: The AV node briefly delays the impulse so the atria can finish emptying into the ventricles
The AV node is the fastest conducting tissue in the heart
Impulses travel from the ventricles upward to the atria
The Purkinje fibers fire before the bundle branches
questions.why: The AV node deliberately slows conduction so atrial contraction can complete ventricular filling before the ventricles contract. It is the slowest conducting tissue, not the fastest, the normal impulse travels downward from atria to ventricles, and the sequence runs from the bundle of His to the bundle branches and then the Purkinje fibers.

questions.q: During a resuscitation you have a lone patient in a narrow hallway with a soft carpeted floor. What is the BEST action before beginning compressions?
choices: Compress in place and press harder to make up for the surface
Move the patient to a firm flat surface with adequate room to work
Place pillows under the shoulders to elevate the chest
Delay compressions until a backboard can be retrieved from the ambulance
questions.why: Effective compressions require a firm surface and space for the team, so a brief controlled move to a hard floor with room to work pays for itself immediately. Pressing harder on a soft surface does not reliably achieve true chest depth because the body sinks. Elevating the shoulders on pillows is not a substitute, and no compressions should be delayed waiting for equipment.

questions.q: A 3-year-old is unresponsive with agonal gasps and no pulse, and you are the only rescuer with no AED yet on scene. What is the FIRST action?
choices: Run to the ambulance to retrieve the AED before starting anything
Attempt five abdominal thrusts in case of an unseen obstruction
Begin CPR at 30 compressions to 2 breaths and call for additional resources
Perform a 30-second pulse recheck to confirm the finding
questions.why: A lone rescuer with a pulseless child begins CPR immediately at 30 to 2 while summoning help, because pediatric arrest is usually hypoxic and compressions plus ventilation are the highest-yield intervention. Leaving to fetch equipment first delays perfusion. Abdominal thrusts are for a conscious choking patient, and the pulse check is limited to 10 seconds and has already been completed.

questions.q: A car strikes a bridge abutment at 55 mph and stops instantly. Which principle BEST explains why the unrestrained driver continues forward into the steering column?
choices: A body in motion stays in motion until acted on by an outside force
Energy is destroyed when the vehicle crushes
Kinetic energy varies only with the mass of the occupant
The driver is protected because the vehicle absorbed all the energy
questions.why: Newton's first law explains that the occupant keeps moving at the vehicle's original speed until something stops him, which is why a second collision occurs between the body and the interior. Energy is not destroyed but converted and transferred. Kinetic energy rises with the square of velocity, so speed matters far more than mass, and vehicle crush absorbs only part of the total energy.

questions.q: An unrestrained driver in a frontal collision followed the up-and-over pathway. Which injury pattern should you suspect FIRST?
choices: Head, facial, cervical spine, and chest injury
Posterior hip dislocation and femur fracture
Bilateral calcaneus fractures
Isolated ankle and foot fractures
questions.why: In the up-and-over pathway the body rises over the steering wheel, driving the head and face into the windshield and the chest into the wheel, so head, neck, and chest injuries lead. Hip dislocation and femur fracture belong to the down-and-under pathway. Calcaneus fractures come from axial loading in falls, not frontal collisions.

questions.q: A restrained driver slid forward and downward under the dash on impact. Which assessment finding is MOST consistent with this mechanism?
choices: Flail segment of the left chest wall
Raccoon eyes and clear nasal drainage
A shortened, internally rotated right leg with knee pain
Paradoxical abdominal breathing
questions.why: The down-and-under pathway drives the knees into the dash, transmitting force up the femur and commonly producing knee injury, femur fracture, and posterior hip dislocation, which presents as a shortened and internally rotated leg. Flail chest and raccoon eyes reflect chest and basilar skull mechanisms. Paradoxical abdominal breathing suggests spinal cord or diaphragmatic problems, not knee loading.

questions.q: A vehicle is struck broadside on the driver's door. Compared with a frontal collision, which injury is MOST likely in this lateral impact?
choices: Bilateral wrist fractures from bracing
Isolated sternal fracture
Posterior hip dislocation
Lateral chest wall and pelvic injury with contralateral neck strain
questions.why: Lateral impact pushes the occupant away from the point of intrusion, injuring the chest wall, shoulder, pelvis, and abdominal organs on the struck side while the head lags and strains the neck. Sternal fracture and posterior hip dislocation are frontal patterns, and bracing wrist fractures are not the primary concern in a T-bone crash.

questions.q: An occupant was ejected from a rolling vehicle. Why does ejection raise your index of suspicion so sharply?
choices: Ejected patients rarely sustain spinal injury
The patient strikes the ground with additional energy transfer and has a markedly higher death rate
Rollover crashes transfer less energy than frontal crashes
Ejection means restraints worked as designed
questions.why: Ejection adds a second impact with the ground or objects and is associated with a dramatically higher mortality, so it is a physiologic-independent trauma alert criterion. Rollovers transfer energy through multiple unpredictable impacts rather than fewer. Spinal injury is more, not less, likely after ejection, and ejection indicates restraints were absent or failed.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man fell from a roof. At what fall height does a fall alone meet significant mechanism criteria for an adult?
choices: More than 6 feet
More than 10 feet
More than 20 feet or three times the patient's height
More than 40 feet
questions.why: Current field triage guidance flags adult falls greater than 20 feet, roughly three times body height, as a significant mechanism warranting trauma center consideration. Six and 10 feet are below that threshold for adults, and waiting for 40 feet would miss many severely injured patients.

questions.q: A 4-year-old fell from a second-story window. Which fall height meets significant mechanism criteria for a child?
choices: More than 10 feet or two to three times the child's height
More than 20 feet only
Any fall from standing height
More than 30 feet
questions.why: For children the threshold is lower, greater than 10 feet or two to three times the child's height, because a proportionally larger head and lower body mass mean less energy is needed to cause serious injury. Applying the adult 20-foot rule to a child under-triages, and treating every standing-level fall as a trauma alert over-triages.

questions.q: After an explosion, a patient has no external wounds but complains of ear pain and increasing shortness of breath. Which blast phase MOST likely caused his injury?
choices: Tertiary, from being thrown against a wall
Primary, from the pressure wave striking gas-filled organs
Secondary, from flying debris
Quaternary, from burns and toxic inhalation
questions.why: Primary blast injury is caused by the overpressure wave and damages air-filled organs such as the tympanic membranes, lungs, and bowel, often with no visible external trauma. Secondary injury comes from projectiles, tertiary from the body being thrown, and quaternary from burns, crush, and inhaled toxins, all of which usually leave visible findings.

questions.q: Which statement BEST describes why a high-velocity rifle wound causes more tissue damage than a low-velocity handgun wound?
choices: Rifle bullets are always larger in diameter
Higher velocity creates temporary cavitation that injures tissue well beyond the bullet track
Handgun wounds cause more cavitation because the bullet tumbles
Exit wounds are always absent with rifle rounds
questions.why: Kinetic energy rises with the square of velocity, so high-velocity rounds produce a temporary cavity that stretches and tears tissue far from the visible path. Bullet diameter is less important than speed, low-velocity rounds cause mainly direct crush injury, and rifle rounds frequently do produce exit wounds.

questions.q: A restrained passenger wearing only a lap belt was in a frontal crash. Which injury is MOST closely associated with this restraint pattern?
choices: Bilateral clavicle fractures
Tension pneumothorax
Isolated scalp laceration
Lumbar spine and abdominal hollow organ injury
questions.why: A lap belt worn alone allows the torso to jackknife forward, compressing abdominal organs against the spine and producing lumbar flexion fractures and hollow organ rupture. Clavicle injury is typical of shoulder harness loading, and tension pneumothorax and scalp lacerations are not characteristic lap-belt patterns.

questions.q: A critically injured trauma patient has an unstable airway and signs of shock. What is the target on-scene time?
choices: 10 minutes or less
20 minutes
30 minutes
Whatever time is needed to complete all interventions on scene
questions.why: Critical trauma patients need definitive surgical care, so the goal is a scene time of 10 minutes or less with only life-saving interventions performed before transport. Longer scene times delay hemorrhage control the EMT cannot provide. Non-critical interventions such as splinting can be done en route.

questions.q: Which facility designation provides the HIGHEST level of definitive trauma care with 24-hour in-house surgical capability and research and teaching commitments?
choices: Level IV
Level III
Level II
Level I
questions.why: A Level I trauma center offers the most comprehensive care, with immediate in-house surgical specialists and required research and education programs. Level II provides comparable clinical care without the research requirement, Level III offers initial stabilization and surgery with transfer arrangements, and Level IV provides stabilization and transfer only.

questions.q: Which situation MOST clearly justifies requesting a helicopter for a trauma patient?
choices: A stable patient with an isolated closed forearm fracture 5 minutes from the hospital
Any patient involved in a rollover collision
A critical multi-system trauma patient trapped in a rural location 45 minutes by ground from the nearest trauma center
A patient who requests air transport
questions.why: Air medical transport is justified when it meaningfully shortens time to definitive care for a critically injured patient, typically long ground transport or prolonged extrication. Short transports, mechanism alone without physiologic or anatomic criteria, and patient preference do not justify the added cost and risk of flight.

questions.q: You approach a patient with a spurting thigh wound who is awake and talking. What is your FIRST action?
choices: Apply a cervical collar
Obtain a full set of vital signs
Control the massive hemorrhage
Perform a head-to-toe secondary assessment
questions.why: Life-threatening external hemorrhage is addressed before airway in the modern trauma primary assessment because exsanguination kills fastest and the patient's speech already shows a patent airway. Collars, vital signs, and the secondary assessment all follow once bleeding is controlled.

questions.q: During a rapid trauma assessment, the B and T in DCAP-BTLS stand for which findings?
choices: Burns and tenderness
Bleeding and tension
Bruising and thrombus
Blisters and trauma
questions.why: DCAP-BTLS stands for deformities, contusions, abrasions, punctures or penetrations, burns, tenderness, lacerations, and swelling. Bleeding, tension, thrombus, and blisters are not the terms in this memory aid, though bleeding is of course assessed separately and immediately.

questions.q: A patient has steady bleeding from a forearm laceration. What is the MOST appropriate initial action?
choices: Apply a tourniquet immediately
Elevate the arm and compress a proximal pressure point
Pack the wound with hemostatic gauze
Apply firm direct pressure over the wound with a sterile dressing
questions.why: Direct pressure with a sterile dressing controls the large majority of external bleeding and is the first step for a bleed that is not immediately life-threatening. Elevation and pressure points are outdated as primary techniques and are no longer taught as effective substitutes. A tourniquet or hemostatic gauze is reserved for bleeding that direct pressure fails to control.

questions.q: Direct pressure fails to control arterial bleeding from a mid-forearm wound. Where should the tourniquet be placed?
choices: Directly over the wound
2 to 3 inches proximal to the wound and not over a joint
Over the elbow joint to compress the brachial artery
As high on the shoulder as possible in all cases
questions.why: A tourniquet is applied 2 to 3 inches proximal to the wound and never over a joint, because bone and joint contours prevent adequate arterial compression. Placing it on the wound will not occlude inflow. Routinely going high and tight is a tactical option when the wound cannot be seen, not the standard for a visible forearm bleed.

questions.q: You are tightening a commercial tourniquet on an injured leg. What endpoint tells you it is tight enough?
choices: The patient reports significant pain
The dressing beneath it is saturated
Bleeding stops and the distal pulse is no longer palpable
The windlass has been turned exactly two full turns
questions.why: The correct endpoint is cessation of bleeding with loss of the distal pulse, which confirms arterial inflow is occluded. Pain is expected but is not the endpoint, continued saturation means it is too loose, and a fixed number of turns ignores differences in limb size. A partially tightened tourniquet can worsen bleeding by occluding only venous return.

questions.q: Fifteen minutes after you applied a tourniquet, bleeding is controlled and your partner asks whether to loosen it briefly. What is the MOST appropriate response?
choices: Leave it in place, note and communicate the application time, and do not loosen it
Loosen it every 10 minutes to perfuse the limb
Remove it once bleeding has stopped for 5 minutes
Cover it with the blanket so the patient cannot see it
questions.why: Once applied and effective, a tourniquet stays on and the application time is written down and reported, because loosening can restart lethal bleeding and release harmful metabolites. Periodic loosening is an obsolete practice. The tourniquet should remain visible and clearly marked so hospital staff do not miss it.

questions.q: A patient has heavy bleeding from a deep wound in the groin where a tourniquet cannot be placed. What is the BEST hemorrhage control technique?
choices: Apply a pressure dressing and elevate the legs
Apply a tourniquet around the pelvis
Apply an occlusive dressing and tape on four sides
Pack the wound with hemostatic gauze and hold firm direct pressure for at least 3 minutes
questions.why: Junctional wounds at the groin, axilla, and neck are not amenable to a limb tourniquet, so wound packing with hemostatic gauze plus at least 3 minutes of uninterrupted direct pressure is the technique of choice. A simple pressure dressing rarely reaches the bleeding vessel, a pelvic tourniquet is not a device, and occlusive dressings do not stop arterial bleeding.

questions.q: A conscious adult has a spontaneous anterior nosebleed. Which instruction is MOST appropriate?
choices: Tilt the head back and pinch the bridge of the nose
Lean forward and pinch the fleshy part of the nostrils together
Lie supine and pack both nostrils tightly
Apply ice to the back of the neck and tilt the head back
questions.why: Leaning forward while pinching the soft portion of the nose compresses the bleeding vessels and keeps blood from draining into the airway and stomach. Tilting the head back causes swallowed blood, vomiting, and possible aspiration. Pinching the bony bridge applies pressure in the wrong place.

questions.q: A 30-year-old was struck in the left flank during a fight. He is pale and anxious with a heart rate of 124 and no external bleeding. These findings MOST likely indicate what?
choices: A simple muscle contusion
An anxiety reaction to the assault
Internal hemorrhage with compensated shock
Neurogenic shock from a spinal injury
questions.why: Pallor, anxiety, and tachycardia without visible bleeding point to internal hemorrhage with the body compensating through vasoconstriction and increased heart rate. A contusion alone should not produce these systemic signs. Neurogenic shock classically produces warm, dry skin with a slow or normal heart rate rather than tachycardia and pallor.

questions.q: A 7-year-old struck by a car has a heart rate of 150, delayed capillary refill, and a blood pressure of 96/70. Which interpretation is MOST accurate?
choices: The child is in compensated shock and a normal blood pressure does not rule it out
The child is stable because the blood pressure is normal for age
The findings indicate mild dehydration rather than blood loss
Hypotension always appears before tachycardia in children
questions.why: Children compensate powerfully and maintain blood pressure until roughly 30 percent or more of blood volume is lost, so tachycardia and poor perfusion define compensated shock even with a normal pressure. Waiting for hypotension means recognizing shock only after decompensation has begun. The narrow pulse pressure here further supports significant blood loss.

questions.q: Which intervention is MOST important in preventing worsening of trauma-induced coagulopathy during transport?
choices: Administering oral fluids for thirst
Placing the patient in a full Trendelenburg position
Massaging cold extremities to restore circulation
Removing wet clothing and keeping the patient warm with blankets
questions.why: Hypothermia impairs clotting enzymes and platelet function and is part of the lethal triad with acidosis and coagulopathy, so aggressive warming and removing wet clothing protect the patient's ability to clot. Oral fluids risk aspiration in a possible surgical patient, Trendelenburg is no longer recommended for shock, and massaging extremities does nothing for core temperature.

questions.q: A worker's fingers were completely amputated by a saw. How should the amputated parts be cared for during transport?
choices: Place them directly on ice to preserve tissue
Submerge them in cool sterile water
Wrap them in dry gauze and leave them at ambient temperature
Wrap them in sterile moist gauze, seal them in a plastic bag, and keep the bag cool but not directly on ice
questions.why: Moist sterile wrapping in a sealed bag kept cool preserves the tissue for possible reimplantation while preventing freeze injury. Direct ice contact and submersion cause frostbite and maceration that make reimplantation impossible. Dry gauze at room temperature allows the tissue to desiccate and deteriorate.

questions.q: A stabbing victim has a segment of bowel protruding through an abdominal wound. What is the MOST appropriate management?
choices: Gently replace the bowel into the abdomen and bandage
Cover with a moist sterile dressing and then an occlusive covering, flexing the patient's knees
Apply a dry bulky dressing and tape it tightly
Pack the wound with hemostatic gauze
questions.why: Eviscerated organs are covered with moist sterile dressing to prevent drying and then an occlusive layer to retain moisture and heat, with knees flexed to reduce abdominal wall tension. Replacing the bowel risks contamination and further injury. Dry or tight dressings dry and damage the exposed tissue, and hemostatic packing is not indicated.

questions.q: A patient has a nail impaled through the cheek with the point protruding into the mouth and blood accumulating in the airway. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Remove the object, control bleeding from both sides, and manage the airway
Stabilize the nail in place with bulky dressings and transport supine
Push the object completely through the cheek
Apply an occlusive dressing over the external end
questions.why: The cheek is the recognized exception to leaving impaled objects in place, because the object itself threatens the airway and bleeding cannot otherwise be controlled from both surfaces. Stabilizing it supine allows continued airway compromise. Pushing an object through causes additional injury and is never appropriate.

questions.q: A patient has a flap of skin torn loose from the forearm that remains attached along one edge. This injury is BEST described as which type?
choices: Abrasion
Contusion
Laceration
Avulsion
questions.why: An avulsion is a flap of skin or tissue torn loose but often still partially attached, which should be replaced in its normal position and dressed. An abrasion is a superficial scrape, a contusion is closed bruising, and a laceration is a cut through the skin without a flap.

questions.q: A patient has a sucking chest wound from a gunshot to the right anterior chest. Which dressing is MOST appropriate?
choices: A dry sterile gauze dressing taped on all four sides
A commercial vented chest seal or an occlusive dressing taped on three sides
A moist sterile dressing
A bulky pressure dressing held with a circumferential wrap
questions.why: A vented chest seal, or an occlusive dressing secured on three sides, blocks air entry during inhalation while allowing trapped air to escape, reducing the risk of tension pneumothorax. Gauze is not occlusive and lets air enter the pleural space. Sealing on four sides without a vent can trap air and create tension physiology.

questions.q: After you apply an occlusive dressing to an open chest wound, the patient becomes more dyspneic and hypotensive with decreasing breath sounds on that side. What should you do NEXT?
choices: Apply a second occlusive dressing over the first
Remove the dressing permanently and leave the wound open
Briefly lift a corner of the dressing to burp it, then reassess
Begin chest compressions
questions.why: These findings suggest a developing tension pneumothorax under the seal, and lifting one corner allows the trapped air to escape and pressure to fall. Adding a second dressing makes the trapping worse. Leaving the wound completely open recreates the open pneumothorax, and compressions are not indicated in a patient with a pulse.

questions.q: Which set of findings is MOST consistent with a developing tension pneumothorax?
choices: Absent breath sounds on one side, distended neck veins, and hypotension
Bilateral crackles, bradycardia, and hypertension
Muffled heart tones with a normal chest x-ray appearance on exam
Symmetrical breath sounds with tracheal deviation as the earliest sign
questions.why: Unilateral absent breath sounds, jugular venous distention from impaired venous return, and hypotension are the classic early field findings of tension pneumothorax. Tracheal deviation is a late and often absent sign, not the first clue. Bilateral crackles suggest pulmonary edema, and muffled heart tones with JVD point toward cardiac tamponade.

questions.q: A 9-year-old was struck in the chest by a falling beam. A section of the anterior chest moves inward during inhalation. What does this finding indicate and why is it concerning in a child?
choices: A simple rib contusion that needs only pain control
A pneumothorax that requires an occlusive dressing
Normal accessory muscle use during distress
Flail chest with paradoxical motion, and children can have severe pulmonary contusion even without rib fractures
questions.why: Inward movement of a chest segment on inhalation is paradoxical motion from a flail segment, and the underlying pulmonary contusion is the true threat to oxygenation. Pediatric ribs are cartilaginous and flexible, so serious lung injury can exist with few or no fractures. This is not accessory muscle use, and an occlusive dressing is for an open wound.

questions.q: A stab wound to the left chest produces hypotension, jugular venous distention, and muffled heart sounds. What condition do these findings describe?
choices: Tension pneumothorax
Simple pneumothorax
Cardiac tamponade
Hemothorax
questions.why: Hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart tones are Beck's triad and indicate pericardial tamponade restricting ventricular filling. Tension pneumothorax also causes JVD and hypotension but with absent breath sounds rather than muffled tones. Hemothorax produces diminished breath sounds with flat, not distended, neck veins from blood loss.

questions.q: A 12-year-old is struck in the chest by a baseball and immediately collapses pulseless. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Apply an occlusive dressing to the chest and transport
Begin high-quality CPR and apply the AED immediately
Perform a rapid trauma assessment before any intervention
Assume internal bleeding and focus on rapid transport without CPR
questions.why: This is commotio cordis, in which a blow during a vulnerable point of the cardiac cycle causes ventricular fibrillation in a structurally normal heart. Early CPR and prompt defibrillation are the only interventions that restore a pulse, and survival falls sharply with delay. Assessment or transport without resuscitation wastes the narrow window.

questions.q: A patient thrown from a motorcycle has pelvic pain, and gentle palpation reveals instability with signs of shock. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Repeatedly rock the pelvis to confirm instability
Apply a traction splint to both legs
Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters and limit further manipulation
Log roll the patient several times to inspect the pelvis
questions.why: A binder placed over the greater trochanters closes the pelvic ring and limits internal hemorrhage, which can be several liters. Repeated rocking disrupts clots and worsens bleeding, so the pelvis is assessed once and gently. Traction splints are contraindicated with a pelvic fracture, and repeated rolling causes additional movement of the unstable ring.

questions.q: A patient kicked in the abdomen holds his knees drawn up and has rigid, tender abdominal muscles with pain in the left shoulder. What do these findings MOST likely indicate?
choices: A simple abdominal wall bruise
Anxiety causing muscle tension
A strained diaphragm from the impact
Intra-abdominal bleeding with peritoneal irritation and referred pain
questions.why: Involuntary guarding with rigidity indicates peritoneal irritation from blood or intestinal contents, and left shoulder pain is classic referred pain from diaphragmatic irritation associated with splenic injury. A superficial bruise does not cause rigidity or referred pain, and attributing these findings to anxiety or muscle strain dangerously delays transport.

questions.q: Two hours after a crush injury to the lower leg, a patient has severe pain out of proportion to the injury, pain on passive stretch, and numbness in the foot. What should you suspect?
choices: Simple muscle cramping from immobility
Compartment syndrome, a true limb-threatening emergency
A healing hematoma requiring only ice
Deep vein thrombosis
questions.why: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, paresthesia, and later pallor, pulselessness, and paralysis are the six Ps of compartment syndrome, which requires urgent surgical fasciotomy. Cramping and hematomas do not produce progressive neurologic deficits. Pulses often remain present early, so waiting for pulselessness delays recognition.

questions.q: Before and after splinting any extremity injury, which assessment must be performed and documented?
choices: Blood glucose in the affected limb
Range of motion through the injured joint
Distal pulse, motor function, and sensation
Circumference measurement of the limb
questions.why: Checking distal pulse, motor function, and sensation before and after splinting detects neurovascular compromise caused or worsened by the splint. Moving the injured joint through range of motion causes further damage. Glucose and limb circumference provide no information about perfusion or nerve function distal to the injury.

questions.q: Which patient is the BEST candidate for a traction splint?
choices: An isolated closed mid-shaft femur fracture with an intact distal pulse
A femur fracture with an associated unstable pelvic fracture
A fracture of the distal tibia and ankle
A posterior knee dislocation
questions.why: Traction splints are indicated for isolated mid-shaft femur fractures, where traction reduces muscle spasm, bleeding, and pain. Pelvic fracture, hip or knee injury, and lower leg or ankle injury are contraindications because traction pulls against an unstable structure or worsens the distal injury.

questions.q: A patient fell on an outstretched arm and has pain and deformity over the right clavicle with good distal circulation. Which immobilization is MOST appropriate?
choices: Traction splint to the arm
Long board immobilization
Rigid splint from wrist to shoulder with the arm extended
Sling and swathe with the arm supported against the chest
questions.why: A sling supports the weight of the arm and a swathe secures it to the chest, immobilizing the clavicle and shoulder girdle comfortably. Traction splints are for the femur only. Extending the arm in a rigid splint increases pain and does not control shoulder motion, and a backboard does nothing for this isolated injury.

questions.q: A severely angulated mid-shaft tibia fracture has no palpable distal pulse and a cool, pale foot. Transport time is 35 minutes. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Splint the limb exactly as found and transport
Apply gentle longitudinal traction to realign the limb, then reassess the pulse and splint
Apply a tourniquet above the fracture
Wait on scene for the pulse to return before moving the patient
questions.why: When distal circulation is absent in an angulated long bone fracture, one gentle attempt at realignment with longitudinal traction may restore perfusion and should be followed by reassessment and splinting. Splinting as found leaves the limb ischemic during a long transport. A tourniquet has no role without hemorrhage, and delaying on scene wastes limb-salvage time.

questions.q: A head-injured patient's vitals change from 130/80 with a pulse of 88 to 186/70 with a pulse of 48 and irregular breathing. What does this indicate?
choices: Compensated hypovolemic shock
An expected response to pain
Cushing's triad indicating rising intracranial pressure
Neurogenic shock from a cervical injury
questions.why: Rising blood pressure with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular respirations form Cushing's triad, a late and ominous sign of increasing intracranial pressure. Hypovolemic shock produces the opposite pattern of tachycardia with falling pressure. Neurogenic shock causes hypotension, not hypertension.

questions.q: A trauma patient opens his eyes to painful stimulus, makes incomprehensible sounds, and withdraws from pain. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
questions.why: Eye opening to pain scores 2, incomprehensible sounds score 2, and withdrawal from pain scores 4, for a total of 8. A score of 8 or less generally indicates a patient who cannot protect the airway. Miscounting usually comes from confusing withdrawal, which is 4, with localizing pain, which is 5.

questions.q: A patient struck in the head has bruising behind the ear and clear fluid draining from the nose. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Pack the nostril firmly to stop the drainage
Have the patient blow the nose to clear the fluid
Apply direct pressure over the bruised mastoid area
Place a loose sterile dressing to absorb the drainage and transport with the head neutral
questions.why: Battle's sign with clear rhinorrhea suggests a basilar skull fracture with cerebrospinal fluid leak, and the drainage must be allowed to flow freely to avoid raising intracranial pressure and to reduce infection risk. Packing or blowing the nose can force contamination intracranially. Pressure over a skull fracture site risks further injury.

questions.q: Using modern selective spinal motion restriction criteria, which patient MOST clearly requires immobilization?
choices: An alert, sober patient in a minor collision with no pain and full painless range of motion
A patient who is intoxicated with midline cervical tenderness after a rollover
A patient with an isolated ankle sprain and no neck complaints
A patient with a hand laceration who is anxious about a lawsuit
questions.why: Intoxication is a distracting and unreliable-exam factor, and midline cervical tenderness after a significant mechanism is a positive finding, so spinal motion restriction is indicated. An alert, sober patient with no tenderness, no neurologic deficit, and no distracting injury can be cleared in the field. Immobilizing everyone causes pressure injury, respiratory compromise, and pain without benefit.

questions.q: An intubated-scope aside, you are bag-mask ventilating an adult head-injury patient with a GCS of 6 and no signs of herniation. What ventilation rate is MOST appropriate?
choices: 20 breaths per minute to lower intracranial pressure
6 breaths per minute to avoid gastric distention
10 breaths per minute, a normal rate, avoiding hyperventilation
30 breaths per minute continuously
questions.why: Head-injured patients are ventilated at a normal rate of about 10 breaths per minute in adults, because hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction and worsens ischemia. Controlled hyperventilation is reserved for clear signs of herniation such as a blown pupil with posturing. Underventilation raises carbon dioxide and also increases intracranial pressure.

questions.q: Using the adult rule of nines, what total body surface area is burned when the entire anterior trunk and one entire arm are involved?
choices: 27 percent
18 percent
36 percent
22.5 percent
questions.why: The adult anterior trunk is 18 percent and one entire arm is 9 percent, totaling 27 percent. Eighteen percent counts only the trunk, and 36 percent would require both the anterior and posterior trunk. In the adult scheme each leg is 18 percent, the head is 9 percent, and the genitalia are 1 percent.

questions.q: How does the pediatric rule of nines differ from the adult version for an infant?
choices: The head is 9 percent and each leg is 18 percent, as in adults
The arms are counted as 18 percent each
Each leg is 9 percent and the trunk is 36 percent
The head is 18 percent and each leg is about 13.5 percent
questions.why: Infants and small children have proportionally larger heads and smaller legs, so the head counts for about 18 percent and each leg for about 13.5 percent. Using adult percentages underestimates burn size in a child and can delay appropriate fluid and burn center referral. Arm values remain 9 percent each.

questions.q: A patient has partial and full thickness burns to about 30 percent of the body. After stopping the burning process, what is the MOST appropriate dressing?
choices: Wet sheets soaked in cool sterile water
Dry sterile dressings or a clean dry sheet, with the patient kept warm
Ice packs applied directly to the burned skin
Antibiotic ointment covered with plastic wrap
questions.why: Large burns lose the skin's thermal barrier, so dry sterile coverings plus active warming prevent dangerous hypothermia. Wet dressings on extensive burns accelerate heat loss and are reserved for small burns. Ice causes further tissue injury, and ointments interfere with hospital burn assessment.

questions.q: A patient rescued from a house fire has singed nasal hairs, soot around the mouth, and a hoarse voice. What is your greatest concern?
choices: Depth of the skin burns on the arms
Carbon monoxide poisoning only
Progressive airway swelling requiring early aggressive airway management and rapid transport
Delayed onset of infection from the burns
questions.why: Soot, singed hairs, and hoarseness signal inhalation injury, and upper airway edema can close the airway rapidly, so high-flow oxygen and immediate transport for definitive airway control take priority. Skin burn depth and infection are important but not immediately lethal. Carbon monoxide is a real concern but does not replace the airway threat.

questions.q: A worker has dry chemical powder on the forearm and reports burning pain. What is the FIRST action?
choices: Brush the dry powder off the skin, then flush with copious water for at least 20 minutes
Flush immediately with water while the powder is still on the skin
Apply a neutralizing acid or base to the area
Cover the area with a dry dressing and transport without irrigation
questions.why: Dry chemicals are brushed away first because water can activate the powder and intensify the burn, then the area is irrigated with large volumes of water for at least 20 minutes. Attempting chemical neutralization creates an exothermic reaction and additional injury. Transporting without irrigation allows the chemical to keep burning.

questions.q: A patient has a laceration to the side of the neck with bleeding and a sucking sound during inhalation. Which action is MOST appropriate?
choices: Apply a circumferential pressure dressing around the neck
Pack the wound with hemostatic gauze and leave it uncovered
Apply a dry gauze dressing and elevate the head of the cot
Apply an occlusive dressing with direct pressure, avoiding pressure on both carotids
questions.why: An open neck vein can entrain air and cause an air embolism, so an occlusive dressing with direct manual pressure over the wound is required. A circumferential dressing can obstruct the airway and compromise cerebral blood flow. Plain gauze is not occlusive, and leaving the wound open to air continues the embolism risk.

questions.q: A woman at 34 weeks gestation was in a collision and is immobilized supine. She becomes pale and hypotensive. What should you do NEXT?
choices: Sit her fully upright to relieve pressure
Tilt the board 15 to 30 degrees to the left or manually displace the uterus to the left
Remove spinal precautions and place her prone
Withhold oxygen to avoid fetal toxicity
questions.why: In late pregnancy the supine uterus compresses the inferior vena cava and reduces venous return, so left lateral tilt or manual uterine displacement restores preload while preserving spinal precautions. Prone positioning and abandoning immobilization are unsafe. Oxygen is beneficial for both mother and fetus, and the fetus can be in distress before the mother shows obvious signs of shock.

questions.q: You are assessing a 58-year-old man with generalized weakness. Which mnemonic BEST organizes the history of the present illness for his complaint of chest discomfort?
choices: SAMPLE
AVPU
OPQRST
DCAP-BTLS
questions.why: OPQRST (onset, provocation, quality, radiation, severity, time) explores the pain or discomfort itself. SAMPLE is the broader patient history, AVPU grades mental status, and DCAP-BTLS is a trauma exam memory aid, so none of those explore the pain characteristics.

questions.q: A medical patient is hypotensive, tachycardic, and confused. How often should you repeat the reassessment during transport?
choices: Every 5 minutes
Every 15 minutes
Only on arrival at the hospital
Every 30 minutes
questions.why: Unstable patients are reassessed at least every 5 minutes; stable patients every 15 minutes. Waiting 15 or 30 minutes, or until arrival, would miss deterioration in a patient who is already showing signs of shock.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman is found confused at home. Using AEIOU-TIPS, which of the following is NOT a cause of altered mental status represented in that mnemonic?
choices: Infection
Overdose
Uremia
Ischemic bone marrow suppression
questions.why: AEIOU-TIPS covers alcohol, epilepsy, insulin, overdose, uremia, trauma, infection, psychiatric, and stroke or shock. Bone marrow suppression is not part of the mnemonic, while infection, overdose, and uremia all are.

questions.q: A 44-year-old man smells strongly of alcohol and is confused. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Assume intoxication and transport without further assessment
Check a blood glucose level and perform a full assessment
Withhold oxygen because alcohol depresses respirations
Have law enforcement take him for detoxification
questions.why: The odor of alcohol never explains altered mental status by itself; hypoglycemia, head injury, hypoxia, and stroke all present the same way. Assuming intoxication or handing the patient to police risks missing a treatable emergency, and oxygen is never withheld from a hypoxic patient.

questions.q: A 67-year-old woman has sudden right-sided facial droop and slurred speech. Which piece of history is MOST critical for the receiving stroke center?
choices: Her current blood pressure
The time she was last known well
Her list of allergies
Whether she has had a stroke before
questions.why: Thrombolytic and thrombectomy eligibility is driven by the last known well time, so it must be obtained and reported. Blood pressure, allergies, and prior strokes matter but do not determine the treatment window.

questions.q: Which three elements make up the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale?
choices: Pupils, grip strength, gait
Speech, blood pressure, glucose
Balance, vision, pronator drift
Facial droop, arm drift, abnormal speech
questions.why: The Cincinnati scale tests facial droop, arm drift, and speech abnormality. Balance and vision belong to the expanded BE-FAST assessment, and pupils, glucose, and blood pressure are separate findings rather than parts of this scale.

questions.q: A 61-year-old man has left-sided weakness and confusion. His glucose reads 38 mg/dL. What does this MOST likely indicate?
choices: Hypoglycemia mimicking a stroke
An evolving hemorrhagic stroke
A transient ischemic attack
Diabetic ketoacidosis
questions.why: Hypoglycemia is a classic stroke mimic and can produce focal deficits that resolve with glucose, which is why glucose is checked on every suspected stroke. DKA causes high glucose, and a stroke or TIA would not explain a reading of 38 mg/dL.

questions.q: Your suspected stroke patient is alert but has a noticeable facial droop and asks for a drink of water. What is the BEST response?
choices: Give small sips of water only
Give water mixed with oral glucose
Give nothing by mouth and explain why
Allow water if she can hold the cup herself
questions.why: Stroke patients frequently have impaired swallowing and are kept NPO to prevent aspiration and to preserve eligibility for hospital interventions. Sips, glucose, or self-feeding do not remove the aspiration risk.

questions.q: A patient's stroke-like symptoms completely resolved after about 20 minutes. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Cancel transport since symptoms resolved
Have the patient follow up with a doctor in a week
Transport only if symptoms return en route
Transport and report a suspected transient ischemic attack
questions.why: A TIA is a warning sign with a high short-term risk of completed stroke, so the patient is transported and evaluated urgently. Refusing or delaying transport because symptoms resolved is a common and dangerous error.

questions.q: Which statement about stroke treatment windows is MOST accurate for EMT reporting purposes?
choices: Thrombolytics may be given up to 12 hours after onset
Thrombectomy is never an option after 6 hours
IV thrombolytics are generally given within 3 to 4.5 hours, with thrombectomy possible up to 24 hours in selected patients
No stroke treatment exists outside of 60 minutes
questions.why: The standard IV thrombolytic window is roughly 3 to 4.5 hours from last known well, and mechanical thrombectomy can be offered up to 24 hours in carefully selected patients. The other options misstate both windows and could cause an EMT to under-prioritize transport.

questions.q: A 26-year-old is having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on a tile floor. What is your FIRST action?
choices: Insert an oral airway to protect the tongue
Protect the head and move nearby objects away
Restrain the arms to stop the shaking
Apply a nonrebreather mask immediately
questions.why: During the active seizure, protect the patient from injury by padding the head and clearing hazards. Never place anything in the mouth or restrain the limbs, and airway and oxygen management comes once the convulsion stops.

questions.q: A patient has been seizing continuously for 8 minutes. This condition is BEST described as:
choices: A febrile seizure
A focal aware seizure
A prolonged postictal state
Status epilepticus
questions.why: Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or repeated seizures without a return to consciousness between them. It is a true emergency because of hypoxia and acidosis, unlike a postictal state, which follows a seizure that has already stopped.

questions.q: A patient's seizure has ended and she is snoring and unresponsive. What is the BEST position and action?
choices: Sit her upright and offer oral glucose
Place her supine with a cervical collar
Place her in the recovery position and manage the airway
Keep her prone with the head turned
questions.why: Left lateral recumbent positioning lets secretions drain and reduces aspiration risk during the postictal period, along with a jaw thrust or head tilt as needed. Oral glucose is unsafe in an unresponsive patient, and prone positioning impairs both airway access and chest expansion.

questions.q: A 14-month-old had a brief generalized seizure with a temperature of 103.2 F. The child is now alert and clinging to the mother. What is the MOST appropriate care?
choices: Place the child in an ice water bath
Keep the child comfortable, remove excess clothing, and transport
Withhold transport since febrile seizures are benign
Hyperventilate the child with a bag-valve mask
questions.why: Simple febrile seizures are managed with passive cooling, airway monitoring, and transport for evaluation of the fever source. Ice baths cause shivering and can worsen things, and a first febrile seizure still warrants evaluation.

questions.q: A college student briefly lost consciousness after standing quickly in a hot lecture hall and awoke within seconds. This event is MOST consistent with:
choices: A focal seizure
A transient ischemic attack
Syncope
Hypoglycemia
questions.why: Syncope is a brief loss of consciousness from transient reduced cerebral perfusion, often vasovagal or orthostatic, with rapid full recovery. Seizures leave a postictal period, TIA causes focal deficits, and hypoglycemia does not resolve on its own in seconds.

questions.q: A 20-year-old with type 1 diabetes is pale, cool, and diaphoretic, with a glucose of 52 mg/dL. He is alert and can follow commands. What is the MOST appropriate treatment?
choices: Assist with his insulin injection
Withhold treatment and transport quietly
Give sips of water only
Administer 15 to 24 g of oral glucose
questions.why: An alert patient who can swallow and protect the airway should receive oral glucose for hypoglycemia. Giving insulin would deepen the hypoglycemia, and withholding sugar risks seizure and unconsciousness.

questions.q: A diabetic patient is unresponsive with a glucose of 40 mg/dL. What is the MOST appropriate EMT action?
choices: Place oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
Pour juice slowly into the mouth
Manage the airway, provide oxygen, and transport rapidly with ALS
Wait for the patient to wake up before acting
questions.why: Nothing is placed in the mouth of an unresponsive patient because of aspiration risk, even glucose gel. Airway support, oxygenation, and rapid transport with ALS for IV dextrose or glucagon is correct.

questions.q: A 32-year-old has deep rapid respirations, fruity breath odor, and reports several days of frequent urination and thirst. Which condition is MOST likely?
choices: Hypoglycemic reaction
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hyperventilation syndrome
Opioid overdose
questions.why: Kussmaul respirations, acetone or fruity breath, polyuria, and polydipsia over days are classic for DKA with hyperglycemia. Hypoglycemia comes on in minutes with cool diaphoretic skin, and opioid overdose slows rather than deepens breathing.

questions.q: Which glucose range is generally considered normal for an adult?
choices: 80 to 120 mg/dL
30 to 60 mg/dL
150 to 200 mg/dL
200 to 300 mg/dL
questions.why: Roughly 80 to 120 mg/dL is the accepted normal range, with hypoglycemia usually defined below 70 mg/dL. The other ranges describe hypoglycemia or significant hyperglycemia rather than normal values.

questions.q: Which statement BEST distinguishes type 1 from type 2 diabetes?
choices: Type 1 occurs only in adults
Type 1 results from little or no insulin production, while type 2 involves insulin resistance
Type 2 always requires insulin injections
Type 1 patients never develop ketoacidosis
questions.why: Type 1 is a failure of insulin production and type 2 is primarily cellular resistance to insulin. Type 1 usually begins in youth, many type 2 patients use oral agents, and DKA is in fact most common in type 1.

questions.q: A 30-year-old stung by a bee has hives, wheezing, and a blood pressure of 78/44. What is the FIRST priority?
choices: Apply ice to the sting site
Give an oral antihistamine
Wait for ALS before any medication
Administer epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in the lateral thigh
questions.why: Hives plus airway compromise or hypotension defines anaphylaxis, and intramuscular epinephrine in the lateral thigh is the immediate lifesaving treatment. Ice, oral antihistamines, and waiting for ALS all delay the only drug that reverses the reaction.

questions.q: A 6-year-old weighing 20 kg is in anaphylaxis. Which auto-injector dose is MOST appropriate?
choices: 0.3 mg
1 mg
questions.why: The pediatric epinephrine auto-injector delivers 0.15 mg IM and is used for children roughly 15 to 30 kg. The 0.3 mg dose is the adult device, and 1 mg is a cardiac arrest IV dose never given by auto-injector.

questions.q: Five minutes after epinephrine, your anaphylaxis patient still has stridor and a pressure of 80/50. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Withhold further epinephrine since one dose was given
Give the patient water to soothe the throat
Place the patient in a sitting position and reassess in 20 minutes
Repeat epinephrine per protocol and continue high-flow oxygen
questions.why: Repeat dosing at 5 to 15 minute intervals is standard when symptoms persist, along with oxygen and rapid transport. Withholding a repeat dose or simply waiting allows continued airway swelling and shock.

questions.q: A patient's anaphylaxis symptoms resolved completely after her own auto-injector. She refuses transport. What is the BEST explanation to give her?
choices: She is fine now and can stay home
She only needs to call if hives return
Symptoms can return hours later in a biphasic reaction, so she should be evaluated
Epinephrine provides 24 hours of protection
questions.why: Biphasic reactions can recur hours after apparent resolution, so every patient who receives epinephrine should be transported and observed. Epinephrine wears off in minutes, not a day.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four routes of poisoning?
choices: Ingestion
Metabolism
Injection
Absorption
questions.why: The four routes are ingestion, inhalation, injection, and absorption. Metabolism is how the body processes a substance after it has already entered, not a route of entry.

questions.q: You arrive to find a 22-year-old unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 4. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: Stimulant overdose
Alcohol withdrawal
Opioid overdose
Organophosphate exposure
questions.why: Pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, and unresponsiveness form the classic opioid triad. Stimulants cause dilated pupils and agitation, withdrawal causes tremor and tachycardia, and organophosphates add the SLUDGE secretions.

questions.q: After ventilating an opioid overdose patient, you give naloxone. What is the correct endpoint of treatment?
choices: Full alertness and ability to walk
Adequate spontaneous breathing
Complete reversal of all sedation
Pupil dilation to 6 mm
questions.why: The goal of naloxone is restoring adequate ventilation, not full arousal, since aggressive reversal can trigger violent withdrawal and combativeness. Typical dosing is 2 mg intranasal or 0.4 to 2 mg IM, titrated to breathing.

questions.q: Activated charcoal is being considered for an ingestion. Which finding is an absolute contraindication?
choices: Ingestion occurred 20 minutes ago
The patient has a decreased level of consciousness
The patient ingested a handful of pills
The patient weighs 70 kg
questions.why: Charcoal, dosed about 1 g/kg where protocols still allow it, requires an alert patient who can protect the airway; altered mental status, caustic or petroleum ingestion, and vomiting are contraindications. Recent ingestion and pill form are actually the scenario where it might be considered.

questions.q: A farm worker is found drooling, incontinent, vomiting, and tearing after spraying pesticide. Which exposure is MOST likely?
choices: Carbon monoxide
Organophosphate
Tricyclic antidepressant
Acetaminophen
questions.why: Salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, and emesis, the SLUDGE or DUMBELS pattern, is characteristic of cholinergic organophosphate poisoning. Carbon monoxide causes headache and confusion, and the drug overdoses listed do not produce massive secretions.

questions.q: A family is found with headache, nausea, and confusion in a home with a running generator. Pulse oximetry reads 99 percent. What is the BEST interpretation?
choices: Oxygenation is normal, so consider another cause
Pulse oximetry can read falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning
The readings prove the patients are malingering
The oximeter is broken and should be replaced
questions.why: Standard pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so readings look normal despite severe hypoxia. Treat with high-flow oxygen, remove patients from the source, and do not be reassured by the number.

questions.q: A 48-year-old who stopped drinking 3 days ago is tremulous, hallucinating, febrile, and tachycardic. This presentation is MOST consistent with:
choices: Acute alcohol intoxication
A stimulant overdose
Hepatic encephalopathy
Delirium tremens
questions.why: Delirium tremens appears roughly 48 to 96 hours after the last drink with tremor, hallucinations, autonomic instability, and seizure risk, and it can be fatal. Intoxication would show sedation rather than this hyperadrenergic picture.

questions.q: A teenager intentionally took an unknown number of acetaminophen tablets 2 hours ago and looks completely well. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Release the patient since there are no symptoms
Have the patient drink milk and call in the morning
Transport for evaluation because serious liver injury is delayed
Induce vomiting with syrup of ipecac
questions.why: Acetaminophen toxicity is deceptively silent early, with hepatic failure developing over 24 to 72 hours, so the well-appearing patient still needs emergency evaluation and levels. Ipecac is no longer used in prehospital care.

questions.q: Which overdose is MOST associated with widened QRS complexes, seizures, and dysrhythmias?
choices: Benzodiazepines
Acetaminophen
Antihistamines alone
Tricyclic antidepressants
questions.why: Tricyclic antidepressants cause sodium channel blockade producing QRS widening, seizures, hypotension, and lethal dysrhythmias, so they warrant early ALS. Benzodiazepine overdose is mainly sedating and acetaminophen affects the liver.

questions.q: When managing a poisoning where the substance is unclear, which resource is MOST appropriate to contact early?
choices: The pharmacy that filled the prescription
The patient's primary care office
Poison control
The local fire marshal
questions.why: Poison control provides immediate, substance-specific guidance and works with medical direction. A pharmacy or primary care office cannot provide toxicologic emergency management in real time.

questions.q: A 19-year-old has periumbilical pain that migrated to the right lower quadrant with nausea and low-grade fever. Which condition is MOST likely?
choices: Cholecystitis
Kidney stone
Pancreatitis
Appendicitis
questions.why: Pain that begins around the umbilicus and localizes to the right lower quadrant with fever and anorexia is classic appendicitis. Cholecystitis is right upper quadrant after fatty meals, pancreatitis radiates to the back, and kidney stones cause flank pain radiating to the groin.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder after a fatty meal. This referred pain pattern MOST suggests:
choices: Cholecystitis
Appendicitis
Diverticulitis
Ovarian torsion
questions.why: Gallbladder inflammation classically refers pain to the right scapula or shoulder and follows fatty meals. The other conditions cause lower abdominal or pelvic pain without this shoulder referral pattern.

questions.q: A 60-year-old reports vomiting material that looks like coffee grounds and black tarry stools. This BEST indicates:
choices: Lower GI bleeding from hemorrhoids
Bowel obstruction
Upper GI bleeding
Acute pancreatitis
questions.why: Coffee-ground emesis and melena reflect blood digested by stomach acid, indicating an upper GI source. Bright red rectal bleeding suggests a lower source, and obstruction produces distension and feculent vomiting instead.

questions.q: A 72-year-old man has sudden tearing back pain, a pulsatile abdominal mass, and unequal femoral pulses. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Palpate the mass firmly to confirm it
Give the patient antacids for indigestion
Place him prone to relieve the back pain
Provide oxygen, limit palpation, and transport rapidly
questions.why: This is an abdominal aortic aneurysm until proven otherwise, and repeated or deep palpation risks rupture. Rapid gentle transport to a surgical facility with ALS is the priority, not treating it as indigestion.

questions.q: Your abdominal pain patient lies very still with knees drawn up and has a rigid, board-like abdomen with guarding. This MOST suggests:
choices: Peritonitis
Gastroenteritis
Constipation
Anxiety
questions.why: Rigidity, guarding, and reluctance to move are hallmarks of peritoneal irritation, a surgical emergency. Patients with colicky causes such as kidney stones tend to writhe rather than hold still.

questions.q: A patient with severe abdominal pain asks for a sip of water. What is the MOST appropriate response?
choices: Give small sips of cold water
Keep the patient NPO and explain that surgery may be needed
Offer ice chips only
Give an antacid from your kit
questions.why: Abdominal pain patients are kept NPO because of possible surgery, anesthesia, and vomiting risk. Ice chips and antacids are still oral intake and are not EMT interventions for undifferentiated abdominal pain.

questions.q: A dialysis patient missed his last two sessions and now has weakness, nausea, and shortness of breath. Which complication is MOST concerning?
choices: Hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia with fluid overload
Dehydration
Hyperthermia
questions.why: Missed dialysis allows potassium and fluid to accumulate, producing weakness, dysrhythmias, and pulmonary edema. These patients are typically fluid overloaded rather than dehydrated, and this is a time-critical transport.

questions.q: Bright red blood is spurting from a dialysis patient's arteriovenous fistula site. What is the FIRST action?
choices: Apply a tourniquet above the fistula immediately
Elevate the arm and wait for ALS
Apply direct pressure over the bleeding site
Pack the site with gauze and tape it tightly around the arm
questions.why: Direct pressure is the first step for shunt or fistula bleeding, and it can be substantial because of high flow and anticoagulation. A tourniquet or circumferential tight wrap threatens the access and is reserved for uncontrolled bleeding as a last resort.

questions.q: An 83-year-old woman is newly confused with mild fever and foul-smelling urine. What is the MOST likely cause of her altered mental status?
choices: Urinary tract infection
Normal aging
Early dementia onset overnight
Dehydration from poor fluid intake alone
questions.why: UTIs commonly present in the elderly as acute confusion without classic urinary complaints, and it is a treatable cause. Confusion is never normal aging, and dementia develops gradually rather than overnight.

questions.q: A 16-year-old male has sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain with nausea that began an hour ago. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Apply heat and have him rest at home
Attempt to manually reduce the testicle
Tell him this usually resolves on its own
Transport promptly because testicular torsion is time-sensitive
questions.why: Torsion threatens testicular viability within hours, so prompt transport for surgical evaluation is essential. EMTs do not attempt manual detorsion, and delaying care risks permanent loss.

questions.q: A patient with a history of Graves disease has a temperature of 104 F, heart rate of 160, agitation, and tremor. This BEST describes:
choices: Adrenal crisis
Thyroid storm
Hypoglycemia
Heat exhaustion
questions.why: Thyroid storm is life-threatening hyperthyroidism with hyperthermia, marked tachycardia, agitation, and tremor. Adrenal crisis presents with hypotension and weakness, and heat exhaustion does not cause this level of tachycardia with a thyroid history.

questions.q: A patient on long-term steroids ran out of medication and is now weak, nauseated, and hypotensive despite fluids. Which condition should you suspect?
choices: Thyroid storm
Adrenal insufficiency
Hypertensive emergency
Diabetes insipidus
questions.why: Abrupt steroid withdrawal can precipitate adrenal crisis with refractory hypotension, weakness, and vomiting requiring hydrocortisone at the hospital. Thyroid storm causes hypertension and hyperthermia rather than shock.

questions.q: A 12-year-old with sickle cell disease has severe bone pain in both legs. Which supportive care is MOST appropriate for an EMT?
choices: Apply cold packs to the painful limbs
Encourage the child to walk it off
Provide oxygen if hypoxic, keep the patient warm, position of comfort, and transport
Restrict all fluids
questions.why: Vaso-occlusive crisis care focuses on oxygenation when indicated, warmth, comfort, hydration, and analgesia at the hospital. Cold causes further vasoconstriction and sickling, and restricting fluids worsens the crisis.

questions.q: A patient with hemophilia struck his forearm and has a rapidly growing hematoma with only a small abrasion. What is the BEST understanding of this patient?
choices: He is exaggerating a minor injury
Minor trauma can cause major internal bleeding, so transport for factor replacement
Hemophilia only affects external bleeding
Direct pressure is unnecessary in hemophilia
questions.why: Clotting factor deficiency means seemingly trivial trauma can produce dangerous internal or joint bleeding requiring factor replacement. Direct pressure is still applied, and internal bleeding is in fact the greater threat.

questions.q: An elderly patient on warfarin fell and struck her head. She is alert with no complaints. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Transport and inform the hospital of the anticoagulation and head strike
Advise her to rest and call if a headache develops
Have her take extra warfarin to prevent clots
Clear her from transport since she is alert
questions.why: Anticoagulated patients can develop delayed intracranial bleeding while looking normal initially, so transport and imaging are warranted. Advising home observation or altering her medication is outside scope and dangerous.

questions.q: A nursing home patient has a temperature of 102.6 F, heart rate of 124, respirations of 26, and blood pressure of 86/50. This combination MOST suggests:
choices: Simple influenza
Anxiety
Dehydration alone
Sepsis
questions.why: Fever with tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension indicates sepsis, a time-critical condition needing early notification and rapid transport. Flu or anxiety would not typically produce this degree of hypotension.
