questions.q: You are transporting a patient with suspected meningitis who has fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. Which precaution is MOST appropriate?
choices: Standard precautions only
Surgical mask on you and the patient plus standard precautions
Full airborne isolation with a powered respirator is required by law
No precautions since meningitis is not contagious
questions.why: Bacterial meningitis spreads by droplets, so masking both provider and patient plus gloves and eye protection is appropriate. Standard precautions alone are insufficient, and meningitis is definitely transmissible.

questions.q: Which action BEST describes standard precautions?
choices: Treating the blood and body fluids of every patient as potentially infectious
Using gloves only for patients with a known infection
Wearing an N95 for every patient contact
Skipping handwashing if gloves were worn
questions.why: Standard precautions assume all blood and body fluids are infectious regardless of diagnosis. Selective glove use, universal N95 use, and skipping hand hygiene after glove removal all misapply the concept.

questions.q: A 24-year-old states she wants to end her life and has a specific plan. What is the MOST appropriate EMT approach?
choices: Leave her alone to calm down
Challenge the plan to show it will not work
Ask directly about the plan and means, ensure scene safety, and do not leave her alone
Promise to keep what she says a secret
questions.why: Asking directly about suicidal intent does not plant the idea and is essential to risk assessment, along with removing means and continuous observation. Confidentiality cannot be promised when safety is at risk, and leaving her alone is dangerous.

questions.q: You must restrain a combative patient with law enforcement. Which practice is correct?
choices: Restrain the patient prone with hands behind the back
Restrain supine or on the side, monitor the airway, and document frequently
Cover the patient's face to reduce spitting and stimulation
Restrain the chest tightly to limit movement
questions.why: Prone restraint, face covering, and chest compression all contribute to positional asphyxia and death. Patients are restrained supine or laterally with continuous airway and breathing monitoring and documented reassessments.

questions.q: A young man is agitated, sweating profusely, undressing, and shouting with a temperature of 104 F and enormous strength. This presentation MOST suggests:
choices: A simple panic attack
Excited delirium requiring rapid ALS, cooling, and monitoring
Intentional malingering
Uncomplicated intoxication
questions.why: Excited delirium features hyperthermia, extreme agitation, pain insensitivity, and high risk of sudden cardiac arrest, and requires rapid sedation by ALS plus cooling. Treating it as panic or malingering delays life-saving care.

questions.q: A patient is behaving bizarrely at a bus stop. What should you consider FIRST?
choices: That the behavior is purely psychiatric
That an organic medical cause such as hypoglycemia, hypoxia, or head injury may be responsible
That police should transport instead
That the patient is faking for attention
questions.why: Behavioral emergencies are frequently medical in origin, so glucose, oxygen saturation, and a trauma survey come before labeling anything psychiatric. Assuming a psychiatric cause is the most common and most dangerous shortcut.

questions.q: Which technique BEST reflects verbal de-escalation of an agitated patient?
choices: Standing very close and maintaining constant intense eye contact
Raising your voice to establish authority
Speaking calmly, keeping a safe distance, and offering realistic choices
Telling the patient the restraints are already on the way
questions.why: Calm tone, respectful distance, honest simple language, and offering limited choices reduce escalation. Crowding, shouting, or making threats provokes the confrontation you are trying to avoid.

questions.q: A roofer is found confused with hot, dry skin, a temperature of 105 F, and a heart rate of 140. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
choices: Give oral electrolyte fluids and rest in the shade
Wrap him in blankets to prevent shivering
Delay cooling until arrival at the hospital
Begin active cooling and transport rapidly
questions.why: Altered mental status with hot skin and high core temperature is heat stroke, and active cooling with cold packs to the neck, axillae, and groin plus rapid transport is life-saving. Oral fluids are unsafe in a confused patient and warming is the opposite of what is needed.

questions.q: How does heat exhaustion MOST clearly differ from heat stroke?
choices: Heat exhaustion always causes a higher temperature
In heat exhaustion the mental status remains normal and the skin is usually cool and moist
Heat exhaustion causes hot dry skin
Heat exhaustion cannot occur in humid weather
questions.why: Heat exhaustion preserves mental status with pale, cool, moist skin, while heat stroke is defined by altered mental status and a failing thermoregulatory system. Hot dry skin is the heat stroke finding, and humidity actually increases risk.

questions.q: A hiker is pulled from cold water, is unresponsive, and appears lifeless. How long should you assess for a pulse?
choices: 5 seconds
10 seconds
30 to 60 seconds
2 full minutes
questions.why: In profound hypothermia, the pulse can be extremely slow and weak, so palpate for 30 to 60 seconds before concluding it is absent and starting compressions. The usual 10 second check can lead to CPR on a perfusing patient.

questions.q: Which handling principle is MOST important in a severely hypothermic patient?
choices: Massage the extremities vigorously to restore circulation
Handle gently, remove wet clothing, and rewarm slowly
Give hot coffee to warm the core quickly
Immerse the patient in hot water immediately
questions.why: Rough handling can precipitate ventricular fibrillation in a cold heart, so movement is gentle, wet clothing comes off, and rewarming is gradual. Caffeine, alcohol, and rapid immersion are contraindicated.

questions.q: A patient has white, waxy, hard fingertips after hours outdoors and you have a 45 minute transport in a warm ambulance. What is the BEST care?
choices: Rub the fingers briskly to restore feeling
Break any blisters that form
Cover and protect the fingers, do not rub, and rewarm only if refreezing will not occur
Immerse the hand in hot water above 120 F
questions.why: Frozen tissue is fragile, so rubbing causes further injury and blisters are left intact. Rewarming is done only when refreezing is impossible, and water for rewarming is body temperature warm, never hot.

questions.q: A child is pulled from a pool and is apneic with a pulse. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
choices: Begin ventilations with a bag-valve mask
Perform abdominal thrusts to expel water
Place in the recovery position and wait
Start chest compressions
questions.why: Drowning is primarily a hypoxic event, so ventilations are the priority in an apneic patient who still has a pulse. Abdominal thrusts to remove water are not recommended and delay oxygenation, and compressions are not indicated with a pulse.

questions.q: A patient has a honeybee stinger still embedded in the forearm. What is the correct removal technique?
choices: Pull it out with tweezers by the venom sac
Squeeze the site to push the stinger out
Scrape it out with the edge of a card
Leave it and apply a tourniquet
questions.why: Scraping removes the stinger without compressing the attached venom sac. Grasping or squeezing injects more venom, and a tourniquet is never indicated for a sting.

questions.q: A hiker was bitten on the hand by a rattlesnake. Which care is MOST appropriate?
choices: Apply a tight arterial tourniquet above the bite
Cut the wound and apply suction
Pack the entire arm in ice
Keep the patient calm and immobilize the extremity at or below heart level
questions.why: Calm, immobilization, removal of rings, and keeping the bite at or below heart level slow venom spread pending antivenom. Cutting, suction, ice, and arterial tourniquets are discredited and cause additional tissue damage.

questions.q: A swimmer is stung by a jellyfish at the beach. Which initial care is BEST?
choices: Rinse the area with fresh cold water
Rub the area with a towel to remove tentacles
Rinse with seawater or vinegar per protocol and remove tentacles carefully
Apply a tourniquet proximal to the sting
questions.why: Fresh water and rubbing cause undischarged nematocysts to fire, worsening envenomation; seawater or vinegar per local protocol is used instead. Tourniquets have no role in marine stings.

questions.q: An 80-year-old man reports only fatigue and mild nausea. His ECG-capable partner suspects a cardiac cause. What geriatric principle BEST explains this?
choices: Elderly patients always have classic crushing chest pain
Older adults may have a silent MI with atypical symptoms such as weakness or nausea
Nausea in the elderly is always gastrointestinal
Age makes myocardial infarction unlikely
questions.why: Silent or atypical MI is common in the elderly and in diabetics, presenting as fatigue, dyspnea, syncope, or nausea rather than chest pain. Dismissing these symptoms as GI or age-related misses a lethal diagnosis.

questions.q: An elderly patient brings a bag with 14 different prescriptions. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Leave the medications at home to save time
Bring the medications or an accurate list, and consider polypharmacy as a cause of symptoms
Only record the cardiac medications
Ask the patient to stop half of them
questions.why: Polypharmacy commonly causes falls, confusion, and hypotension in older adults, and the hospital needs the full list. Selecting only some medications, or advising the patient to stop any, is incomplete and outside your scope.

questions.q: You notice an elderly woman with poor hygiene, untreated pressure sores, and a caregiver who answers all questions for her and will not leave the room. What is the MOST appropriate response?
choices: Confront the caregiver about suspected abuse
Ignore it since there is no visible injury
Document objective findings, attempt to interview the patient separately, and report per state law
Ask the patient in front of the caregiver if she is being abused
questions.why: EMTs are mandatory reporters in most states and should document observations factually and report through proper channels. Confronting the caregiver or questioning the patient in his presence can escalate danger to the patient.

questions.q: Which three components make up the pediatric assessment triangle?
choices: Pulse, respirations, blood pressure
Appearance, work of breathing, circulation to the skin
Airway, breathing, circulation
Color, capillary refill, temperature
questions.why: The PAT is a from-the-doorway impression using appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to the skin. Vital signs and the ABCs are part of the hands-on assessment that follows, not the triangle itself.

questions.q: A 2-year-old has a barking cough, low-grade fever, and inspiratory stridor that began at night and improves in cool air. Which condition is MOST likely?
choices: Epiglottitis
Bronchiolitis
Asthma
Croup
questions.why: A barking seal-like cough with night onset and improvement in cool air is classic viral croup. Epiglottitis is abrupt with high fever, drooling, and a tripod posture, and bronchiolitis produces wheezing in infants.

questions.q: A 5-year-old sits leaning forward, drooling, with muffled voice and a temperature of 104 F. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Lay the child flat and inspect the throat with a tongue blade
Give the child water to relieve the sore throat
Keep the child calm and upright with blow-by oxygen and transport immediately
Force an oral airway to keep the airway open
questions.why: Suspected epiglottitis demands keeping the child calm in a position of comfort; agitation or anything in the mouth can cause complete airway obstruction. Inspection with a tongue blade is specifically contraindicated.

questions.q: A 5-month-old has wheezing, nasal congestion, tachypnea, and poor feeding during the winter. Which condition is MOST likely?
choices: Bronchiolitis
Croup
Foreign body aspiration
Pertussis
questions.why: Bronchiolitis, usually from RSV, causes wheezing, congestion, tachypnea, and feeding difficulty in infants during the winter. Croup produces stridor and a barking cough rather than diffuse wheezing.

questions.q: Which finding is the MOST reliable early sign of significant dehydration in a 1-year-old?
choices: Bright red cheeks
Increased appetite
Loud crying
Decreased wet diapers with dry mucous membranes and delayed capillary refill
questions.why: Reduced urine output, dry mucous membranes, sunken fontanelle, and delayed capillary refill reliably indicate dehydration. A vigorous cry and good appetite actually argue against significant volume loss.

questions.q: A 3-week-old is lethargic, feeding poorly, and has a temperature of 100.6 F. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Advise the parents to give infant acetaminophen and observe at home
Transport immediately because fever in a young infant may indicate sepsis
Wait to see whether the temperature rises
Assume teething is the cause
questions.why: Any fever in an infant under about 2 months, especially with lethargy and poor feeding, is treated as possible sepsis or meningitis and requires immediate evaluation. Teething does not cause fever plus lethargy at this age.

questions.q: Parents report their 6-week-old briefly turned blue, went limp, and then recovered fully. She now looks normal. This event is BEST described as:
choices: A febrile seizure
A brief resolved unexplained event requiring transport
Normal infant breathing
Sudden infant death syndrome
questions.why: A BRUE involves a brief episode of color change, tone change, or altered breathing with full recovery, and it still requires evaluation because a serious cause may underlie it. SIDS by definition involves death, and no fever or seizure was described.

questions.q: You respond to a 4-month-old found unresponsive and pulseless in a crib with obvious dependent lividity and rigor. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Begin CPR regardless and transport emergently
Move the infant immediately to the ambulance before assessing
Follow protocol regarding obvious death, preserve the scene, and support the family
Tell the parents the infant suffocated on bedding
questions.why: With definitive signs of death such as rigor and lividity, resuscitation is generally not initiated per protocol, the scene is preserved for investigators, and the family receives compassionate support. EMTs do not speculate aloud about the cause.

questions.q: A toddler has circular burns on the buttocks with sharply defined edges and a history that keeps changing. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Treat the burns, transport, document objectively, and report your suspicion per law
Accuse the caregiver at the scene
Refuse to transport until police arrive
Record the caregiver's explanation as fact and take no further action
questions.why: EMTs are mandatory reporters and should document observations objectively, treat the injuries, transport, and report suspicions through the proper channel. Accusations at the scene can endanger the child and the crew.

questions.q: Which structure exchanges oxygen and nutrients between the mother and fetus?
choices: Amniotic sac
Fundus
Cervix
Placenta
questions.why: The placenta transfers oxygen, nutrients, and waste between maternal and fetal circulation. The amniotic sac cushions the fetus, the cervix is the uterine opening, and the fundus is the upper uterine dome.

questions.q: A 34-week pregnant woman becomes dizzy and hypotensive when lying flat on the stretcher. What is the BEST action?
choices: Elevate her legs and keep her supine
Sit her fully upright with legs dangling
Place her in Trendelenburg
Place her on her left side or wedge the right hip
questions.why: Supine hypotensive syndrome occurs when the gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava, and left lateral positioning or a right hip wedge relieves it. Remaining supine in any variation, including Trendelenburg, maintains the compression.

questions.q: A pregnant patient tells you she is gravida 3, para 1. What does this mean?
choices: She has been pregnant three times and has had one delivery reaching viability
She has three living children and one miscarriage
She is in her third trimester and first labor
She has had three deliveries and one pregnancy
questions.why: Gravida counts total pregnancies and para counts pregnancies carried to viable delivery. The other options confuse para with living children or with trimester and labor descriptions.

questions.q: Which change is a normal physiologic finding in late pregnancy?
choices: A resting heart rate of 40
Blood volume increases by roughly 40 to 50 percent
Blood pressure of 160/100 is expected
Respiratory rate of 6
questions.why: Maternal blood volume rises about 40 to 50 percent, which means a pregnant patient can lose significant blood before showing shock signs. Bradycardia, hypoventilation, and hypertension above 140/90 are abnormal and concerning.

questions.q: An 8-week pregnant woman has severe left lower quadrant pain, vaginal spotting, and a pressure of 88/52 with a heart rate of 126. Which condition is MOST likely?
choices: Normal early pregnancy discomfort
Placenta previa
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Preeclampsia
questions.why: Unilateral lower abdominal pain with early pregnancy, spotting, and shock strongly suggests a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, which is a surgical emergency. Previa and preeclampsia are late-pregnancy problems and would not cause this early picture.

questions.q: A woman at 30 weeks has painless, bright red vaginal bleeding without contractions. Which condition is MOST likely?
choices: Abruptio placentae
Placenta previa
Uterine rupture
Spontaneous abortion
questions.why: Painless bright red bleeding in the later trimesters suggests placenta previa, where the placenta covers the cervical os. Abruption is typically painful with dark bleeding and a rigid, tender uterus.

questions.q: A 36-week pregnant woman in a minor collision now has constant severe abdominal pain, a rigid uterus, and dark vaginal bleeding. Which condition is MOST likely?
choices: Placenta previa
Braxton Hicks contractions
Normal labor
Abruptio placentae
questions.why: Painful dark bleeding with a rigid, tender abdomen after trauma is classic placental abruption, and concealed bleeding can make the external loss underestimate the severity. Previa is painless and labor contractions are intermittent rather than constant rigidity.

questions.q: A woman at 33 weeks has a blood pressure of 162/104, facial and hand edema, a severe headache, and visual changes. What is the BEST management?
choices: Encourage her to walk to improve circulation
Give her oral fluids and reassess in 30 minutes
Transport calmly and quietly with minimal stimulation, monitor closely, and notify the hospital
Have her lie flat and apply bright lights to check pupils
questions.why: These findings are severe preeclampsia, and stimulation can precipitate eclamptic seizures, so a dim, quiet transport with close monitoring and early notification is correct. Oral fluids, ambulation, and bright light all add risk or delay.

questions.q: A pregnant woman with known preeclampsia begins seizing during transport. Her condition is now called:
choices: Gestational diabetes
Eclampsia
Hyperemesis gravidarum
Supine hypotensive syndrome
questions.why: Preeclampsia that progresses to seizures is eclampsia, which threatens both mother and fetus and requires airway protection, left lateral positioning, and rapid transport with ALS. The other conditions do not cause seizures.

questions.q: A woman at 9 weeks has had intractable vomiting for days and is now weak with dry mucous membranes. This is MOST consistent with:
choices: Hyperemesis gravidarum
Normal morning sickness
Gestational diabetes
Spontaneous abortion
questions.why: Hyperemesis gravidarum is persistent vomiting causing dehydration, weight loss, and electrolyte disturbance, requiring IV fluids. Ordinary morning sickness does not produce this degree of dehydration, and no bleeding was described to suggest miscarriage.

questions.q: Which set of findings BEST indicates that delivery is imminent and you should prepare to deliver on scene?
choices: Contractions 10 minutes apart with intact membranes
Back pain and nausea in the third trimester
Crowning with contractions about 2 minutes apart and a strong urge to push
A first pregnancy with contractions that began an hour ago
questions.why: Crowning, contractions roughly 2 minutes apart, and an urge to push mean delivery is happening now and transport should not be attempted. Contractions 10 minutes apart or recent onset in a first pregnancy usually allow time to transport.

questions.q: As the newborn's head delivers, you feel the umbilical cord looped around the neck. What is the BEST action?
choices: Push the head back in until the cord frees
Gently slip the cord over the head, and if it cannot be freed, clamp in two places and cut between
Pull firmly on the cord to break it
Ignore it and continue delivery
questions.why: A nuchal cord is first gently slipped over the head; only if it is too tight is it clamped twice and cut between the clamps to allow delivery. Pushing the head back or pulling the cord causes serious injury.

questions.q: Immediately after delivery, which action is MOST important for the newborn?
choices: Dry, warm, and stimulate the newborn, positioning the airway
Suction the mouth and nose routinely for two minutes
Clamp the cord within 10 seconds
Weigh the newborn before any other care
questions.why: Drying, warmth, and stimulation with airway positioning are the priorities because newborns lose heat rapidly and usually respond to stimulation alone. Routine deep suctioning is no longer recommended and weighing is irrelevant in the field.

questions.q: Which newborn vital signs are within normal limits at 5 minutes of life?
choices: Heart rate 140, respirations 48
Heart rate 70, respirations 12
Heart rate 190, respirations 70
Heart rate 90, respirations 20
questions.why: A normal newborn heart rate is above 100, typically 120 to 160, with respirations of 40 to 60. A rate of 70 or 90 indicates the need for ventilations and possibly compressions, not a normal finding.

questions.q: The APGAR score is assessed at which intervals?
choices: Immediately and at 10 minutes
Every 5 minutes until the hospital
At 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth
Only once, at 5 minutes
questions.why: APGAR scoring for appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, and respiration is performed at 1 and 5 minutes, each item scored 0 to 2 for a maximum of 10. It never delays resuscitation, which is guided by heart rate and respiratory effort.

questions.q: You see the umbilical cord protruding from the vagina before the baby delivers. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Push the cord gently back into the vagina
Clamp and cut the cord immediately
Have the mother stand and walk to the ambulance
Place the mother in knee-chest or Trendelenburg, relieve pressure on the cord with gloved fingers, and transport rapidly
questions.why: A prolapsed cord is compressed by the presenting part, so elevating the hips and holding the presenting part off the cord preserves fetal circulation during rapid transport. Pushing the cord back in or clamping it would kill the fetus.

questions.q: After delivery the mother continues to bleed heavily and has soaked several pads. What is the BEST initial action?
choices: Pack the vagina with trauma dressings
Have her sit upright to slow the bleeding
Massage the fundus, allow the newborn to nurse if possible, and transport rapidly
Wait for the placenta to deliver before doing anything
questions.why: Blood loss above 500 mL is postpartum hemorrhage, and fundal massage plus nursing stimulates uterine contraction to control it. Nothing is ever packed into the vagina, and treatment should not be delayed for the placenta, which is transported with the patient when delivered.

questions.q: A patient needs an IV started and a limited set of medications given during transport. Which level of certification is the LOWEST that may routinely establish peripheral IV access?
choices: Advanced Emergency Medical Technician
Emergency Medical Technician
Emergency Medical Responder
Paramedic only
questions.why: The AEMT is the lowest national level whose scope routinely includes peripheral IV access and a limited medication set. EMRs provide initial stabilizing care with minimal equipment, and EMTs are limited to basic interventions plus assisting with a small list of medications. Paramedic is correct in that they can do it, but the question asks for the lowest level.

questions.q: An EMT administers oral glucose to a hypoglycemic patient using a written protocol without contacting the hospital. This is an example of what?
choices: Offline medical direction through standing orders
Online medical direction
Practicing outside the scope of practice
Implied consent for treatment
questions.why: Standing orders are written protocols issued in advance by the medical director, which is offline (indirect) medical direction. Online direction would require real-time contact by radio or phone. The action is squarely within EMT scope, and consent describes patient permission, not physician authorization.

questions.q: A service reviews a random sample of patient care reports each month, compares findings to protocol, and schedules targeted training. This process is BEST described as what?
choices: Medical direction
Continuous quality improvement
Peer review of licensure
Mandatory reporting
questions.why: Continuous quality improvement is the ongoing, system-wide review of performance with corrective education to improve patient care. Medical direction is physician oversight of practice, mandatory reporting refers to legally required notifications such as suspected abuse, and licensure review is a state regulatory function.

questions.q: An EMT holds a current National Registry credential but has just moved to New Jersey. Which statement is MOST accurate?
choices: National Registry certification alone authorizes practice in any state
The state must still grant certification or licensure before the EMT may practice there
Licensure is issued by the National Registry and certification by the employer
Practice is authorized as soon as an agency hires the EMT
questions.why: National Registry certification verifies competency but does not grant the legal privilege to practice; the state, such as the New Jersey Office of Emergency Medical Services, issues the certification or license that authorizes practice. Employment or agency hiring does not by itself confer legal authority, and the Registry does not issue state licenses.

questions.q: You arrive at a reported assault and see two people actively fighting in the driveway near your patient. What is your FIRST action?
choices: Approach and attempt to separate the combatants
Begin triage of the patient on the ground
Stage at a safe distance and request law enforcement
Retrieve the stretcher so you can move the patient quickly
questions.why: Scene safety precedes patient care; the correct action is to retreat or stage at a safe distance and wait for law enforcement to secure the scene. Entering to separate combatants or beginning care in an active fight exposes the crew to injury and is the classic student error of entering an unsafe scene to help.

questions.q: During size-up of a two-car crash you find four patients, one trapped by a deformed door. Which action is MOST appropriate at this point?
choices: Begin extricating the trapped patient with hand tools
Request additional ambulances and a rescue unit for extrication
Complete assessment of all four before calling anyone
Load the walking patients and transport immediately
questions.why: Determining the number of patients and calling for additional resources early is part of scene size-up, and extra units take time to arrive. Starting extrication without rescue capability, transporting before the scene is organized, or delaying the request until assessments are finished all leave the remaining patients without resources.

questions.q: You are transporting a patient with a productive cough, night sweats, and weight loss who is suspected of having tuberculosis. Which protection is MOST appropriate for the crew?
choices: A fit-tested N95 respirator for each provider and a surgical mask on the patient
Surgical masks for the crew only
Gown and gloves without any mask
A nonrebreather mask on the patient and no crew protection
questions.why: Tuberculosis is spread by the airborne route, so providers need a fit-tested N95 respirator while the patient wears a surgical mask to contain droplet nuclei. A surgical mask does not filter airborne particles for the wearer, and gowns or oxygen devices alone do not address airborne transmission.

questions.q: You are about to suction a patient with copious bloody vomit in the airway. Which combination of standard precautions is BEST?
choices: Gloves only
Gloves, eye protection, and a mask or face shield
Gown and shoe covers only
An N95 respirator alone
questions.why: Splash-generating procedures such as suctioning require barrier protection for the eyes, nose, and mouth in addition to gloves. Gloves alone leave mucous membranes exposed, and an N95 is intended for airborne disease rather than routine splash protection.

questions.q: During a transport an EMT sustains a needlestick from a used catheter stylet. After immediate wound care, what is the NEXT step?
choices: Wait to see whether symptoms develop before saying anything
Ask the patient to volunteer for testing and take no further action
Document it only in the patient care report narrative
Report the exposure to the designated infection control officer and follow the post-exposure plan
questions.why: After washing the site, the exposure must be reported promptly to the designated infection control officer so source testing, prophylaxis, and follow-up can begin within the effective time window. Waiting for symptoms or documenting only in the patient care report delays care and violates the exposure control plan.

questions.q: Which vaccination must an employer make available at no cost to EMS personnel with occupational exposure risk?
choices: Rabies
Yellow fever
Hepatitis B
Hepatitis C
questions.why: Federal bloodborne pathogen rules require employers to offer the hepatitis B vaccine series free of charge to at-risk employees, who may decline in writing. There is no vaccine for hepatitis C, and rabies and yellow fever vaccines are not routine occupational requirements for EMS.

questions.q: Which activity belongs to the preparation phase rather than the en route or post-run phase of an ambulance call?
choices: Notifying dispatch that the unit is responding
Completing the daily vehicle and equipment inspection at shift start
Giving the verbal handoff report to the nurse
Cleaning and restocking the patient compartment after the call
questions.why: The daily inspection of the vehicle, oxygen, and equipment occurs during preparation, before any call is received. Notifying dispatch belongs to the en route phase, the handoff occurs at the hospital, and cleaning and restocking belong to the post-run phase.

questions.q: An ambulance is responding with lights and siren to a cardiac arrest. Which statement about emergency vehicle operation is MOST accurate?
choices: Warning devices ask for the right of way but do not excuse the driver from operating with due regard
Warning devices legally permit any speed the driver judges necessary
Red lights and siren transfer liability for a crash to other motorists
Stop signs may be ignored entirely during a true emergency response
questions.why: Lights and siren only request that other drivers yield; the operator still owes a duty of due regard and remains liable for negligent operation. Exemptions from traffic laws are limited and conditional, so speed, stop signs, and signals still require the driver to slow, confirm, and proceed safely.

questions.q: A police car offers to escort your ambulance through heavy traffic. What is the MOST appropriate response?
choices: Follow closely so you do not lose the escort
Accept and match the escort speed through intersections
Decline the escort, because escorted responses greatly increase intersection crash risk
Accept but turn off your own warning devices
questions.why: Escorts are discouraged because motorists who yield to the first vehicle often pull back out in front of the second, and following closely removes reaction distance. Intersections are the most common site of ambulance collisions, so each vehicle should travel independently and clear intersections separately. Turning off your own warning devices makes the ambulance less visible, not safer.

questions.q: You arrive at an overturned tanker leaking an unknown liquid with a light wind blowing from the north. Where should you position the ambulance?
choices: Downwind and downhill to shield the scene
Directly beside the tanker to shorten the carry
As close as possible so equipment is within reach
Uphill and upwind, well back from the spill
questions.why: Vapors and liquid both travel downhill and downwind, so the safe staging position is uphill and upwind at a distance. Parking close, beside, or downwind places the crew and the ambulance inside the hazard area and can trap the unit if the incident grows.

questions.q: A helicopter is being requested for a rural crash. Which description of the landing zone and approach is correct?
choices: A 50 by 50 foot area, approached from the rear
A 100 by 100 foot area clear of wires, approached from the front in the pilot's view
Any paved surface, approached from whichever side is closest
A 100 by 100 foot area, approached from the tail so the pilot can see you
questions.why: A standard landing zone is at least 100 by 100 feet, level, firm, and free of wires, poles, and loose debris, and crews approach only from the front where the pilot can see them and only when signaled. Approaching from the rear risks the tail rotor, which is nearly invisible when spinning, and a 50 foot zone is too small for a rotorcraft.

questions.q: You are lifting the foot end of a loaded stretcher with your partner. Which technique BEST describes a proper power lift?
choices: Back locked in slight inward curve, feet flat, weight lifted with the legs, load kept close to the body
Knees locked, bending forward at the waist to reach the handle
Arms extended away from the body to clear your legs
One foot forward and a twist at the waist to set the load down
questions.why: The power lift keeps the back straight with its normal inward curve, the feet flat and shoulder width apart, and the load close while the leg muscles do the work. Bending at the waist, holding the load away from the body, or twisting while lifting all multiply spinal load and are the leading causes of EMS back injury.

questions.q: An EMT team of two is asked to move a 380 pound patient down a narrow hallway. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Attempt the lift quickly to limit strain time
Have one EMT lift the torso while the other drags the legs
Use an emergency move so the lift is brief
Request additional personnel and appropriate bariatric equipment before moving the patient
questions.why: Knowing your physical limits and requesting help and proper equipment prevents injury to both crew and patient. Rushing the lift, improvising a two-person drag, or misusing an emergency move when there is no immediate threat all increase the chance of a drop and a career-ending back injury.

questions.q: Fire is spreading toward a car with an unresponsive driver who must be moved immediately. Which technique is MOST appropriate?
choices: Direct ground lift after full spinal immobilization
Extremity lift onto a stair chair
Clothes drag, supporting the head and neck as much as possible
Wait for the fire crew to knock down the flames before touching the patient
questions.why: An immediate life threat such as fire justifies an emergency move, and the clothes drag lets one rescuer pull along the long axis of the body while offering some head and neck support. Non-urgent moves such as the direct ground lift or extremity lift take too long, and waiting leaves the patient in a lethal environment.

questions.q: A stable patient with abdominal pain must be moved from a second-floor bedroom down a narrow staircase. Which device is MOST appropriate?
choices: Stair chair, with the patient secured and carried down
Wheeled cot rolled down the stairs on its wheels
Scoop stretcher carried flat by two rescuers
Long backboard used as a slide down the steps
questions.why: The stair chair keeps the patient in a compact seated position and is the safest device for a narrow staircase when the patient does not require supine positioning. A wheeled cot is not designed to roll down stairs, and carrying a flat scoop or sliding a board down steps is unstable and risks dropping the patient.

questions.q: Before moving the loaded wheeled cot to the ambulance, which securing step is MOST important?
choices: Tighten only the chest and lap straps to save time
Apply all cot straps including the shoulder harnesses
Leave the leg strap loose in case the patient must sit up
Rely on the side rails rather than the straps
questions.why: All manufacturer-supplied straps, including shoulder harness straps, must be applied so the patient cannot slide forward in a sudden stop or collision. Partial strapping and raised side rails do not restrain a patient in a crash, and loosening a strap for convenience defeats the restraint system.

questions.q: A woman in the third trimester of pregnancy becomes lightheaded and hypotensive after being placed supine on the cot. Which position is MOST appropriate?
choices: Trendelenburg with the head lowered
Full Fowler's position
Prone with padding under the abdomen
Left lateral recumbent
questions.why: Turning the patient onto her left side moves the gravid uterus off the inferior vena cava and restores venous return, correcting supine hypotensive syndrome. Trendelenburg and Fowler's positions do not relieve the caval compression, and the prone position is unsafe and prevents assessment.

questions.q: A 2-year-old with a fever is being transported and the mother asks to hold the child in her arms on the bench seat. What is the MOST appropriate response?
choices: Allow it, since the mother will keep the child calm
Allow it if the mother wears the seat belt with the child inside it
Secure the child in an approved child restraint or the cot and seat the mother belted separately
Place the child unrestrained on the cot next to the mother
questions.why: A child held on a caregiver's lap becomes an unrestrained projectile in a crash and can be crushed by the adult's body, so the child must be secured in an appropriate size-rated restraint or properly strapped to the cot. Sharing a seat belt with an adult is never acceptable, and an unrestrained child on the cot is equally unsafe.

questions.q: A patient found supine on the floor has no suspected spinal injury and must be lifted to the cot with two EMTs. Which non-urgent move is MOST appropriate?
choices: Direct ground lift
Firefighter's carry
Blanket drag
Draw sheet transfer
questions.why: The direct ground lift is designed for two or three rescuers to raise a supine patient without suspected spinal injury from the ground to the cot. The blanket drag and firefighter's carry are emergency moves used only with an immediate threat, and the draw sheet is used to transfer a patient between a bed and a cot, not from the floor.

questions.q: After a violent pediatric cardiac arrest call, a veteran EMT becomes irritable, sleeps poorly, and withdraws from the crew. Which action is MOST appropriate?
choices: Tell the EMT to take more overtime to stay busy
Offer critical incident stress management resources and encourage peer support or counseling
Remove the EMT from all patient care permanently
Advise the EMT that these reactions mean unsuitability for EMS
questions.why: Irritability, sleep disturbance, and withdrawal are recognized stress reactions and are addressed through critical incident stress management, peer support, and professional counseling. More work worsens cumulative stress, and permanently removing or labeling the provider is neither supported nor necessary for a normal stress response.

questions.q: A car has come to rest on its side against a tree with a conscious patient inside. What must occur BEFORE crews enter the vehicle?
choices: Removal of the windshield with a saw
Disconnection of the battery by the EMT crew
Stabilization of the vehicle with cribbing or struts
Deflation of all four tires to lower the vehicle
questions.why: An unstable vehicle can shift and injure both the patient and the rescuers, so cribbing, struts, or chocks must stabilize it before anyone enters. Glass removal and battery disconnection come later in the extrication sequence, and deflating tires on a vehicle resting on its side does not create stability.

questions.q: You are working next to an undeployed driver side airbag during an extrication. Which clearance guideline is correct?
choices: Stay at least 2 inches from any airbag module
There is no safe distance once the ignition is off
Only the passenger side airbag poses a hazard
Allow 5 inches for a side airbag, 10 inches for a driver airbag, and 20 inches for a passenger airbag
questions.why: The 5-10-20 inch rule describes the minimum working distances from side, driver, and passenger airbag modules because a late deployment can strike a rescuer. Turning the ignition off does not immediately discharge stored capacitor energy, so the distances still apply, and all airbag locations pose a risk, not just the passenger side.

questions.q: A downed power line lies across the hood of a crashed car with an alert, uninjured occupant inside. What is the BEST action?
choices: Use a dry wooden pole to push the line off the car
Have the occupant step out quickly and run clear
Keep everyone at least one full span outside the downed wires and have the occupant stay in the car until the utility de-energizes the line
Approach the vehicle from the side opposite the wire
questions.why: The safe distance is at least one full span of wire in every direction because an energized line can whip or re-energize and the ground itself can be charged. The occupant is safest remaining in the vehicle until the utility confirms the line is de-energized; stepping out risks completing a circuit through ground gradient, and no improvised tool safely moves a live conductor.

questions.q: You stop several hundred feet from an overturned truck showing a placard with a four-digit number. What should you do FIRST?
choices: Use binoculars to read the placard and UN number, then consult the Emergency Response Guidebook
Move closer to read the placard clearly
Enter and remove any patients before the leak worsens
Begin decontamination of bystanders on the roadway
questions.why: Identification from a safe distance with binoculars and the Emergency Response Guidebook lets you determine the isolation distances before anyone is committed. Moving closer to read the placard or entering to rescue patients places unprotected EMTs inside the hot zone, and decontamination is performed by trained teams in the warm zone corridor.

questions.q: Contaminated patients from a chemical release are being moved toward your ambulance in the cold zone. Which action is MOST appropriate for the EMT?
choices: Begin immediate assessment and treatment before decontamination
Enter the hot zone in a gown and N95 to speed removal
Load contaminated patients into the ambulance and decontaminate en route
Wait for patients to be decontaminated by the hazmat team, then assess and treat in the cold zone
questions.why: EMTs trained to the awareness level do not enter the hot or warm zones, and treating or transporting a contaminated patient spreads the agent to the crew, the ambulance, and the hospital. Care begins after decontamination is complete, in the cold zone, except for interventions the decon team itself is trained to perform.

questions.q: At a bus crash, the incident commander has 14 responders reporting directly. Which action BEST addresses span of control?
choices: Keep direct control so information is not lost
Assign all 14 to a single treatment group without supervisors
Delegate by establishing sections and group supervisors so each supervisor manages about three to seven people
Transfer command to the first arriving ambulance crew
questions.why: NIMS recommends a span of control of three to seven subordinates with five as the ideal, so the commander delegates by creating sections and groups such as triage, treatment, transport, and staging. Retaining 14 direct reports overwhelms the commander, and transferring command to an arriving crew does not solve the structural problem.

questions.q: You are the first EMT on scene at a 20-patient incident and begin START triage. What is the BEST first step?
choices: Announce for anyone who can walk to move to a designated area and tag them green
Start at the closest patient and work outward
Begin CPR on the first pulseless patient you reach
Treat the most dramatic-appearing injuries first
questions.why: START begins by directing ambulatory patients to a collection area, which immediately identifies the minor or green group and reduces the number needing individual evaluation. Working patient by patient from the nearest, beginning CPR, or being drawn to the most dramatic injuries all stall triage and deny care to salvageable patients.

questions.q: During START triage you find an adult who is not breathing. You open the airway and spontaneous respirations begin at 36 per minute. How should this patient be tagged?
choices: Green, minor
Red, immediate
Yellow, delayed
Black, expectant
questions.why: A respiratory rate over 30 meets the immediate criterion, and because breathing returned with a simple airway maneuver the patient is red rather than expectant. Opening the airway is one of only two interventions performed during triage, the other being control of massive bleeding, and the triager then moves on.

questions.q: A 5-year-old at an MCI is apneic after you position the airway but has a palpable pulse. Under JumpSTART, what is the NEXT step?
choices: Tag the child black and move on
Begin full CPR at the scene
Give 5 rescue breaths and reassess for spontaneous respirations
Tag yellow and reassess in 10 minutes
questions.why: JumpSTART accounts for the respiratory cause of most pediatric arrests by allowing 5 rescue breaths for an apneic child who still has a pulse; if breathing resumes the child is tagged red, and if not the child is tagged black. Full CPR is not performed during triage, and tagging an apneic child yellow or black without the breath trial misses a salvageable patient.

questions.q: Triage at a building collapse is complete: 4 red, 7 yellow, 12 green, and 3 black. The first two ambulances arrive. Who should be transported FIRST?
choices: The green patients, to clear the scene quickly
The black-tagged patients, to a trauma center
The yellow patients, since they are stable enough to survive transport
Two of the red, immediate patients
questions.why: Immediate (red) patients have life threats that are survivable with prompt care, so they go first as transport resources arrive. Green patients can wait or be moved by alternative means, yellow patients can tolerate delay, and black-tagged patients are not transported ahead of salvageable ones.

questions.q: Dispatch reports an active shooter in a shopping center with multiple people down. What is the MOST appropriate action for your crew?
choices: Stage in a safe location outside the area and await law enforcement clearance or integration into a rescue task force
Drive to the entrance and begin triage of the closest victims
Enter with law enforcement and begin full trauma care in the hot zone
Park at the doors so victims can self-evacuate to you
questions.why: Unarmed EMS stages away from the scene until law enforcement establishes a secured corridor, and care in the warm zone occurs only as part of a rescue task force with force protection and body armor. Entering a hot zone, or parking at the entrance where the threat and secondary devices are most likely, endangers the crew and creates more victims.

questions.q: An alert, oriented adult with chest pain says clearly that he does not want to go to the hospital. Which action is MOST appropriate?
choices: Transport under implied consent because the complaint is serious
Assess capacity, explain the risks, encourage transport, and document the refusal with the patient's signature and a witness
Have a family member sign the refusal instead of the patient
Restrain the patient for his own safety and transport
questions.why: A competent adult has the right to refuse care even when the decision is unwise; the EMT must confirm capacity, explain the specific risks in plain language, offer transport again, and document the refusal with a patient signature and a witness. Implied consent applies only to patients unable to consent, and transporting or restraining a competent refusing adult constitutes assault, battery, and false imprisonment.

questions.q: A 9-year-old is struck by a car at a park and no parent can be reached. Which legal principle allows treatment and transport?
choices: Expressed consent from a bystander
Emancipation of the minor
Implied consent, because a reasonable parent would consent to emergency care
A court order obtained by the receiving hospital
questions.why: When a parent or guardian is unavailable and the child has an emergency condition, the law presumes a reasonable parent would consent, so care proceeds under implied consent. Bystanders cannot give consent for another person's child, emancipation applies only to minors legally recognized as adults, and waiting for a court order would dangerously delay care.

questions.q: A crew leaves a hypoglycemic patient with a first responder of lower training and departs before transfer to an equal or higher level of care. Which term BEST describes this?
choices: Assault
Battery
Breach of confidentiality
Abandonment
questions.why: Abandonment is terminating care without the patient's consent and without transferring to a provider of equal or greater training. Assault is placing someone in fear of harmful contact, battery is the unlawful contact itself, and confidentiality concerns disclosure of patient information.

questions.q: A 4-year-old has patterned bruising in various stages of healing and a caregiver story that changes with each retelling. What is the MOST appropriate action?
choices: Confront the caregiver and demand an explanation before transporting
Say nothing unless you can prove abuse occurred
Photograph the injuries with your personal phone for evidence
Provide care, transport, document objective findings, and report the suspicion to the proper authority as a mandated reporter
questions.why: EMTs are mandated reporters and must report a reasonable suspicion of child abuse to the designated authority; proof is not required and is not the EMT's job. Confronting the caregiver can escalate the scene and endanger the child, staying silent violates the reporting duty, and personal photographs breach patient privacy.

questions.q: While writing a patient care report you realize you wrote the wrong blood pressure. How should the error be corrected?
choices: Draw a single line through the entry, write the correct value beside it, and initial and date the change
Erase or use correction fluid so the record is clean
Black the entry out completely with marker
Rewrite the entire report and discard the original
questions.why: The legal standard is a single line through the error with the correction, initials, and date so the original entry remains readable. Obliterating, erasing, or discarding an original record looks like falsification and can destroy the report's credibility in court and lead to certification action.

questions.q: Which entry in a patient care report narrative is an OBJECTIVE finding?
choices: The patient appeared to be faking the pain
Skin was cool and diaphoretic, radial pulse 118 and regular
The patient was probably intoxicated
The family seemed uncooperative and difficult
questions.why: Objective findings are measurable or directly observed data such as skin condition and pulse rate, and they belong in the O section of a SOAP or the assessment portion of a CHART narrative. The other entries are opinions and conclusions that are not supported by measured data and can expose the provider to liability; pertinent negatives should also be recorded as observed absences of findings.

questions.q: You are 12 minutes out with a 6-year-old in respiratory distress. Which radio report order is MOST appropriate?
choices: Everything the parents told you, in the order they said it
A request for orders first, then patient details if time allows
Unit identification, age and sex, chief complaint, brief history, vital signs, treatment given, and ETA
The patient's full name, address, and insurance information
questions.why: The standard radio report is concise and follows a predictable order so the receiving facility can prepare, and it is given early enough that staff and equipment can be assembled before arrival. Identifying information such as name and address is not broadcast over the radio, and an unstructured account delays the clinically useful details.

questions.q: A neighbor who called 911 asks what is wrong with the patient you are loading. Which response is MOST appropriate?
choices: Give a brief summary since the neighbor made the call
Provide the hospital destination and the diagnosis only
Share the information if the neighbor is a nurse
Politely decline to share any patient information, because it is protected health information
questions.why: Protected health information may be shared only for treatment, payment, or operations, or with the patient's authorization; a caller or neighbor has no right to it regardless of their profession or involvement. Even the destination and a diagnosis identify the patient's condition and constitute a disclosure, so the EMT declines politely and continues care.
